The cliché of it all is what gets her. The fact that there are literal bloody pearls on the bloody gates, under a perfect blue sky with fluffy clouds floating about. The only thing that doesn’t fit is the desk. It looks like it was ripped from some dentist’s waiting room, glass panels connected to nothing. And a sad looking bloke stuck behind one of three windows. He’s a nondescript little figure, dark brown hair and a black bomber jacket.

“Next,” he says, though there’s no queue, just her. He sounds bored, with an accent she can’t quite place. American.

She steps forward. The floor beneath her shimmers with ethereal light, and squeaks under her trainers.

“Name?”

Screw that. She takes a deep breath. “Is this a dream or a hallucination or… I don’t know – something like that?” Not that she’s ever known she was dreaming before, nor is she prone to hallucinations. Still, it can’t hurt to ask.

“No. You’re dead. No, this isn’t being caused by lack of oxygen to the brain, you’ve made it fully to the other side, and no, you can’t go back. Name?”

“Uh, Alice? Alice B. Clarkson. So is this like – I mean, I wasn’t expecting it to be… Christian.”

He taps away at his all-white box of a computer and squints. “Clarence, Clark, Cl - Clarkson. There you are. Hm. Ok, I’ve got you under atheist, subcategory: pedant. And the ‘B’ really doesn’t stand for anything?” He shakes his head a little before grabbing a form, sliding it under the glass divider. “Alright, fill that in as best you can.”

“I don’t. Have a pen?”

A biro appears.

The first question: ‘From 1 to 10, where 1 is an abiding and unforgivable grudge, and 10 is perfect, harmonious forgiveness, how do you feel about the following people and incidents?

1. Thomas Morrison for biting you at your third birthday party, on April 3rd, 1999.
2. Alexander Clarkson for refusing to buy you ice cream on April 20th, 1999.’

And so on and so forth. She flicks through.

‘Rank the following in the order in which you would choose to live with them in a shared housing situation: Lilian McCarthy, Claire Simons, Aisha Hassan…’

“What is this?” she asks.

The man at the desk sighs. “Eternal bliss? We need to know who to house you near. It’s really not that complicated, just put the names in order.”

“OK,” says Alice. “But I was – am? – an atheist. I don’t – I lost Pascal’s Wager, right? I’m headed downstairs. Right?” She taps the pen, doesn’t quite commit to picking it up, lets it roll in the little well under the divider.

“I mean if you want to, then sure, I can probably sort that.” He goes back to his computer, hits a few keys. F, three times, then I. Then a random assortment of letters, quicker than she can follow, but not spelling out anything, at least as far as she can tell. She can’t see the screen, but there’s no glow on his face. “Okay, it’ll be a bit of a wait. No one’s at reception at the moment but I’ve sent out a ping. It’s a bit empty, and they’re not expecting you, but the team can probably sort you out with somewhere to stay.”

“That’s –” not right, surely? “Dude,” she says. Puts the form down. “I lost.”

He straightens up, looks at her properly for the first time. “Yeah, you did. Turns out it was all real, irrespective of anything you believed or didn’t or anything you ever did. And who’s going to benefit from torturing you for eternity?”

She rubs a heel against the squeaky floor. “I –”

“No one, right? Not me, not you, not the big guy. You can’t go back, that’s the point. You’ve gone down a one-way road. You’ll never be able to tell anyone, ‘I was wrong! It’s all real!’ who doesn’t already know. The wager’s done. So you might as well come in, because why not?”

“Right,” she says. “And then it turns out this is actually the bad place, and hell is other people, and really the perfect torturer is me, myself?”

“That sounds like a lot of work, to be honest with you. I mean, most people tend to just muddle on by, even if things aren’t perfect, that’s all of Earth.”

She finally scoops up the pen. It’s odd – smooth, and there’s text, or something that at least is making an honest attempt to look like text. Right where a brand name should be engraved on the lid. But it’s not. There’s no real letters, just – just squiggles in shapes that letters maybe could make in an alphabet gone slightly to the left.

She blinks and it’s gone, leaving behind plain, unmarred blue plastic. She shrugs it off, and brings it to the page, but before she can even start to write, a 4 appears next to Thomas Morrison’s name.

“Um,” she says. Tries to cross it out. Nothing happens.

The gatekeeper sighs. Again. “Yes?”

“I didn’t –”

“Ah. Apologies, cause and effect should be working properly now.”

“Right,” she says, and this time she can actually scribble out the ‘4’, replace it with a 3.5. The pen behaves itself as she goes through childhood grudges and ex boyfriends and arguments she had in Reddit comment sections. It’s a lot.

“I have a question,” she says, as she rates whether she was attracted to several different individuals, and how she feels about them now.

“I live to serve,” says the clerk.

“How did I die?”

“Drunk driver,” he says. “Not your fault. The funeral was well attended. If you want to see it once you’re set up, someone can track down a recording for you.”

She doesn’t remember it. Doesn’t – where was she before she died? Edinburgh, surely, working on her thesis. Failure points in solar panels. Useful, as she had claimed in her application. But there’s no money in academia. She’s never exactly planned to stay, as she explained herself to her mother. Just to write something.

Still. For all that her life, in hindsight, feels like an exercise in futility, damn whatever bastard decided to jellify her against the roadside.

The clerk pokes at the computer again, as she stands there for a moment. Then she goes back to the form, which appears to have already finished the section she was on and moved on to the next. She clears her throat. No more ink appears.

“So. God’s real?”

“Mmhmm.”

“Evolution?”

“Last I heard, the big guy wishes he came up with it before doing everything by hand.”

“Okay so someone came up with, I don’t know, human genitalia and childhood genetic diseases?” She glances up from the form. “Though I’m sure I’m not the first person to mention the problem of suffering.”

He shrugs. “It’s a reasonable question, though not one with a satisfying answer. I mean, I asked the same thing when I got up here, pretty sure everyone does when they realize it won’t get them kicked out the door.”

“So? What’s the unsatisfying answer?”

“For the genitalia? Extreme jerryrigging. It’s like code; if you take a busy, overworked programmer, obviously you’re going to wind up with an inefficient mess of a solution where everything gets routed together. Can’t sort out temperature control? Guess we’ll just use air to cool the gonads and hope no one decides to kick them.”

He rolls his eyes. “You know, Christianity was 90% right, but they definitely overshot with the whole infallible thing. Plenty of bugs in the code that the big guy’s too lazy to fix.”

“Childhood cancer is a bug in the code?” Alice stares at him. “Not to be Epicurean about it, but that’s – you all seem pretty omnipresent and omnipotent to me, so –”

“Ah well, finite suffering for eternal paradise isn’t the worst trade-off. As a ratio of your total existence, that blip on Earth is infinitesimal, in the most literal sense of the word. It all comes out in the wash.”

“Right,” says Alice, and finds that she dislikes all of this immensely. “I think I will go downstairs, actually, if that’s alright?”

He blinks. “Why?”

She slides the form under the glass and steps back, looking around. The clouds drift in a clockwise circle above her head, though there’s… something about them.

She stares closer. There’s one, the perfect cloud. A normal distribution with lumps in all the right places. A few others, the sorts of clouds made for debates over whether they’re shaped like cows or castles. And then there’s one that’s identical to the first, just reflected over the y-axis and maybe a bit smaller.

Pascal’s Wager. She’s called this asshole’s bluff once already, might as well try what’s already worked once.

“Perhaps I just reject the morality of your system. That’s allowed, isn’t it?”

He stands up, walks out from behind the desk and around to her. Brushes some of his gingery hair out of his face.

“Kiddo, there’s no one else down there. We could arrange some eternal torment, if it’s really what you want, but it’ll take a while to set up and you’ll just be hanging around by yourself for ages. Why not just go on through, we’ll set you up somewhere to live, you’ll see your grandma again. It’ll be perfect.”

“How did I die?” she asks, again. “Because last I remember, I was hosting office hours.”

The desk looks different now.

She squints at it for a second, before it clicks. She couldn’t see her reflection in the glass before. But there she is. And is the computer a different computer?

She blinks. No, it’s the same old white box.

He looks down at her. “Heart attack in your sleep. You wouldn't."

"You said drunk driver." There are, she realizes, four clouds, up to transformation. They're just copies, stretched or shrunk or flipped. "Before, you said it was a drunk driver."

His face goes still for a second, and then he smiles. "Of course. It was traumatic. You wouldn't remember it. Remarkable what the psyche can do to protect itself."

The air suddenly fills with the furious reek of burning rubber, stinging at her nostrils, catching on her palms, on the cuts on her palms as though they’ve skidded over something rough.

She breathes, she tries to breathe but it’s rough and burbling and there’s something wet coming up her throat. Get it out, she needs to get it out, she coughs, but it’s not a cough. Her throat spasm, her lungs hitch but there’s no air, there’s no air there’s nothing coming through she can’t breathe she can’t breathe her heart is shrieking in her useless throat and ears and she can’t

Breathe.

She breathes.

She shakes.

“Like I said,” says the clerk. “The brain doesn’t like to remember trauma.” He holds out a bottle of water that definitely wasn’t in his hand a moment ago. Like the pen, there’s a label on it that could be any of the brands she’s ever seen, but isn’t quite any of them. But she takes it anyway. Drinks. It tastes like water, which is good enough.

Her hand’s shaking, but she’s got to keep her head on straight. “I still want to head downstairs. How long until they’re ready for me?”

He stares at her. The bottle in her hand goes from ribbed, to smooth, back to ribbed again.

“How long?”

“You are aware that you’re signing up for an eternity far worse than what you just experienced?” he asks, flatly.

“Yes.” Does her best to sound confident.

He stares at her. She stares at him. The same four clouds circle overhead. And then he tilts his head, and something sharp sets in behind his eyes. She feels, for a moment, unable to so much as twitch. Like he’s turned her to stone. Then, smoothly he does up a button on his coat, gives a perfect, customer service smile. Bored. Painted on.

“Well, we aim to please. Now, just to be clear, if you go downstairs there’s no coming back up. It’s another one way road.”

“That’s what I assumed. I still want to go.” The water bottle is cool against her hand and she rubs at its ridges. “Now, please.”

He circles back around the desk and sits. “We value informed consent here.”

Her nerves seize all at once. Her legs promptly decide they no longer function as legs and deposit her on the gently glowing linoleum as she spasms, convulses. It’s beyond pain, it’s beyond – her brain, she can feel, repeatedly trying for the off switch but the power stays on.

She twitches over and over in agony that intensifies from impossible to incomprehensible, more than can even be screamed out. The bottle’s gone somewhere, rolled away. She crushed it, maybe, in that first collapse inward.

“It’s been thirty seconds,” says the clerk from the desk. “Halfway through.”

And she lies on that smooth, plastic floor and she suffers.

Passage B:
I got as far as Norway. The first plane out of Newark in the right direction took me to Oslo, which was at least closer to Finland than New York. Perhaps there was some greater hand steering my purpose, that saw the sleeper train up to Trondheim still running on Christmas Eve. Every inch fought northward was a battle, but one the universe seemed to want me to win. Until it didn’t.

We got past Lillehammer before everything ground to a halt. We had a cabin to ourselves, me lying there uselessly with the oxygen tank on the floor next to my bed and Arnie on the top bunk listening to me wheeze away. Good reason to raise hopeless children – if they never manage to find someone willing to marry them, they can follow you north to watch you die.

He swung himself off the bunk and opened the blind. I pushed myself up on my elbows so I could see out – nothing. The odd juddering lantern light, white on the white of the snow, as the staff rushed back and forth along the length of the stopped train.

"The heating's still on," said Arnie, hand over the vent. "Can't be anything too wrong."

He shifted his weight from foot to foot, still standing by the little sink looking out the window.

I wheezed at him for lack of any other response.

"Should I go ask what's going on?" he asked.

"What's that going to help?"

"They could tell us when we'll be moving again?"

High rising terminal. Again. Useless boy. But there was no point in him being here.

"Go on then," I said.

He dithered for a moment, fiddling with the settings on the heating until I waved him away.

“Go.”

I lay back as the door slid open then closed again.

Was that my breathing, or the wind? Both.

Of course he’d come early.

Had he been up there since the train stopped, or had he only arrived once Arnie left? Didn't matter much. He slid his legs over the edge, just like Arnie had done, and down off the bunk. In green, now, wrapped in furs the colour of the forest I caught the edge of as we landed. Smelled like pine and snow and something raw and mammalian. Primitive. Outside, one of the lanterns caught its light on the window, capturing a black-and-white moment of all that picture imperfect snow, and there in front of it: him. His hat. That marketing-ready red that I’d put on him.

"I was going after you," I said.

He leaned over me, staring. I knew what he saw. Withered. Passage B:
The cliché of it all is what gets her. The fact that there are literal bloody pearls on the bloody gates, under a perfect blue sky with fluffy clouds floating about. The only thing that doesn’t fit is the desk. It looks like it was ripped from some dentist’s waiting room, glass panels connected to nothing. And a sad looking bloke stuck behind one of three windows. He’s a nondescript little figure, dark brown hair and a black bomber jacket.

“Next,” he says, though there’s no queue, just her. He sounds bored, with an accent she can’t quite place. American.

She steps forward. The floor beneath her shimmers with ethereal light, and squeaks under her trainers.

“Name?”

Screw that. She takes a deep breath. “Is this a dream or a hallucination or… I don’t know – something like that?” Not that she’s ever known she was dreaming before, nor is she prone to hallucinations. Still, it can’t hurt to ask.

“No. You’re dead. No, this isn’t being caused by lack of oxygen to the brain, you’ve made it fully to the other side, and no, you can’t go back. Name?”

“Uh, Alice? Alice B. Clarkson. So is this like – I mean, I wasn’t expecting it to be… Christian.”

He taps away at his all-white box of a computer and squints. “Clarence, Clark, Cl - Clarkson. There you are. Hm. Ok, I’ve got you under atheist, subcategory: pedant. And the ‘B’ really doesn’t stand for anything?” He shakes his head a little before grabbing a form, sliding it under the glass divider. “Alright, fill that in as best you can.”

“I don’t. Have a pen?”

A biro appears.

The first question: ‘From 1 to 10, where 1 is an abiding and unforgivable grudge, and 10 is perfect, harmonious forgiveness, how do you feel about the following people and incidents?

1. Thomas Morrison for biting you at your third birthday party, on April 3rd, 1999.
2. Alexander Clarkson for refusing to buy you ice cream on April 20th, 1999.’

And so on and so forth. She flicks through.

‘Rank the following in the order in which you would choose to live with them in a shared housing situation: Lilian McCarthy, Claire Simons, Aisha Hassan…’

“What is this?” she asks.

The man at the desk sighs. “Eternal bliss? We need to know who to house you near. It’s really not that complicated, just put the names in order.”

“OK,” says Alice. “But I was – am? – an atheist. I don’t – I lost Pascal’s Wager, right? I’m headed downstairs. Right?” She taps the pen, doesn’t quite commit to picking it up, lets it roll in the little well under the divider.

“I mean if you want to, then sure, I can probably sort that.” He goes back to his computer, hits a few keys. F, three times, then I. Then a random assortment of letters, quicker than she can follow, but not spelling out anything, at least as far as she can tell. She can’t see the screen, but there’s no glow on his face. “Okay, it’ll be a bit of a wait. No one’s at reception at the moment but I’ve sent out a ping. It’s a bit empty, and they’re not expecting you, but the team can probably sort you out with somewhere to stay.”

“That’s –” not right, surely? “Dude,” she says. Puts the form down. “I lost.”

He straightens up, looks at her properly for the first time. “Yeah, you did. Turns out it was all real, irrespective of anything you believed or didn’t or anything you ever did. And who’s going to benefit from torturing you for eternity?”

She rubs a heel against the squeaky floor. “I –”

“No one, right? Not me, not you, not the big guy. You can’t go back, that’s the point. You’ve gone down a one-way road. You’ll never be able to tell anyone, ‘I was wrong! It’s all real!’ who doesn’t already know. The wager’s done. So you might as well come in, because why not?”

“Right,” she says. “And then it turns out this is actually the bad place, and hell is other people, and really the perfect torturer is me, myself?”

“That sounds like a lot of work, to be honest with you. I mean, most people tend to just muddle on by, even if things aren’t perfect, that’s all of Earth.”

She finally scoops up the pen. It’s odd – smooth, and there’s text, or something that at least is making an honest attempt to look like text. Right where a brand name should be engraved on the lid. But it’s not. There’s no real letters, just – just squiggles in shapes that letters maybe could make in an alphabet gone slightly to the left.

She blinks and it’s gone, leaving behind plain, unmarred blue plastic. She shrugs it off, and brings it to the page, but before she can even start to write, a 4 appears next to Thomas Morrison’s name.

“Um,” she says. Tries to cross it out. Nothing happens.

The gatekeeper sighs. Again. “Yes?”

“I didn’t –”

“Ah. Apologies, cause and effect should be working properly now.”

“Right,” she says, and this time she can actually scribble out the ‘4’, replace it with a 3.5. The pen behaves itself as she goes through childhood grudges and ex boyfriends and arguments she had in Reddit comment sections. It’s a lot.

“I have a question,” she says, as she rates whether she was attracted to several different individuals, and how she feels about them now.

“I live to serve,” says the clerk.

“How did I die?”

“Drunk driver,” he says. “Not your fault. The funeral was well attended. If you want to see it once you’re set up, someone can track down a recording for you.”

She doesn’t remember it. Doesn’t – where was she before she died? Edinburgh, surely, working on her thesis. Failure points in solar panels. Useful, as she had claimed in her application. But there’s no money in academia. She’s never exactly planned to stay, as she explained herself to her mother. Just to write something.

Still. For all that her life, in hindsight, feels like an exercise in futility, damn whatever bastard decided to jellify her against the roadside.

The clerk pokes at the computer again, as she stands there for a moment. Then she goes back to the form, which appears to have already finished the section she was on and moved on to the next. She clears her throat. No more ink appears.

“So. God’s real?”

“Mmhmm.”

“Evolution?”

“Last I heard, the big guy wishes he came up with it before doing everything by hand.”

“Okay so someone came up with, I don’t know, human genitalia and childhood genetic diseases?” She glances up from the form. “Though I’m sure I’m not the first person to mention the problem of suffering.”

He shrugs. “It’s a reasonable question, though not one with a satisfying answer. I mean, I asked the same thing when I got up here, pretty sure everyone does when they realize it won’t get them kicked out the door.”

“So? What’s the unsatisfying answer?”

“For the genitalia? Extreme jerryrigging. It’s like code; if you take a busy, overworked programmer, obviously you’re going to wind up with an inefficient mess of a solution where everything gets routed together. Can’t sort out temperature control? Guess we’ll just use air to cool the gonads and hope no one decides to kick them.”

He rolls his eyes. “You know, Christianity was 90% right, but they definitely overshot with the whole infallible thing. Plenty of bugs in the code that the big guy’s too lazy to fix.”

“Childhood cancer is a bug in the code?” Alice stares at him. “Not to be Epicurean about it, but that’s – you all seem pretty omnipresent and omnipotent to me, so –”

“Ah well, finite suffering for eternal paradise isn’t the worst trade-off. As a ratio of your total existence, that blip on Earth is infinitesimal, in the most literal sense of the word. It all comes out in the wash.”

“Right,” says Alice, and finds that she dislikes all of this immensely. “I think I will go downstairs, actually, if that’s alright?”

He blinks. “Why?”

She slides the form under the glass and steps back, looking around. The clouds drift in a clockwise circle above her head, though there’s… something about them.

She stares closer. There’s one, the perfect cloud. A normal distribution with lumps in all the right places. A few others, the sorts of clouds made for debates over whether they’re shaped like cows or castles. And then there’s one that’s identical to the first, just reflected over the y-axis and maybe a bit smaller.

Pascal’s Wager. She’s called this asshole’s bluff once already, might as well try what’s already worked once.

“Perhaps I just reject the morality of your system. That’s allowed, isn’t it?”

He stands up, walks out from behind the desk and around to her. Brushes some of his gingery hair out of his face.

“Kiddo, there’s no one else down there. We could arrange some eternal torment, if it’s really what you want, but it’ll take a while to set up and you’ll just be hanging around by yourself for ages. Why not just go on through, we’ll set you up somewhere to live, you’ll see your grandma again. It’ll be perfect.”

“How did I die?” she asks, again. “Because last I remember, I was hosting office hours.”

The desk looks different now.

She squints at it for a second, before it clicks. She couldn’t see her reflection in the glass before. But there she is. And is the computer a different computer?

She blinks. No, it’s the same old white box.

He looks down at her. “Heart attack in your sleep. You wouldn't."

"You said drunk driver." There are, she realizes, four clouds, up to transformation. They're just copies, stretched or shrunk or flipped. "Before, you said it was a drunk driver."

His face goes still for a second, and then he smiles. "Of course. It was traumatic. You wouldn't remember it. Remarkable what the psyche can do to protect itself."

The air suddenly fills with the furious reek of burning rubber, stinging at her nostrils, catching on her palms, on the cuts on her palms as though they’ve skidded over something rough.

She breathes, she tries to breathe but it’s rough and burbling and there’s something wet coming up her throat. Get it out, she needs to get it out, she coughs, but it’s not a cough. Her throat spasm, her lungs hitch but there’s no air, there’s no air there’s nothing coming through she can’t breathe she can’t breathe her heart is shrieking in her useless throat and ears and she can’t

Breathe.

She breathes.

She shakes.

“Like I said,” says the clerk. “The brain doesn’t like to remember trauma.” He holds out a bottle of water that definitely wasn’t in his hand a moment ago. Like the pen, there’s a label on it that could be any of the brands she’s ever seen, but isn’t quite any of them. But she takes it anyway. Drinks. It tastes like water, which is good enough.

Her hand’s shaking, but she’s got to keep her head on straight. “I still want to head downstairs. How long until they’re ready for me?”

He stares at her. The bottle in her hand goes from ribbed, to smooth, back to ribbed again.

“How long?”

“You are aware that you’re signing up for an eternity far worse than what you just experienced?” he asks, flatly.

“Yes.” Does her best to sound confident.

He stares at her. She stares at him. The same four clouds circle overhead. And then he tilts his head, and something sharp sets in behind his eyes. She feels, for a moment, unable to so much as twitch. Like he’s turned her to stone. Then, smoothly he does up a button on his coat, gives a perfect, customer service smile. Bored. Painted on.

“Well, we aim to please. Now, just to be clear, if you go downstairs there’s no coming back up. It’s another one way road.”

“That’s what I assumed. I still want to go.” The water bottle is cool against her hand and she rubs at its ridges. “Now, please.”

He circles back around the desk and sits. “We value informed consent here.”

Her nerves seize all at once. Her legs promptly decide they no longer function as legs and deposit her on the gently glowing linoleum as she spasms, convulses. It’s beyond pain, it’s beyond – her brain, she can feel, repeatedly trying for the off switch but the power stays on.

She twitches over and over in agony that intensifies from impossible to incomprehensible, more than can even be screamed out. The bottle’s gone somewhere, rolled away. She crushed it, maybe, in that first collapse inward.

“It’s been thirty seconds,” says the clerk from the desk. “Halfway through.”

And she lies on that smooth, plastic floor and she suffers.

“Right,” she says. “And then it turns out this is actually the bad place, and hell is other people, and really the perfect torturer is me, myself?”

“That sounds like a lot of work, to be honest with you. I mean, most people tend to just muddle on by, even if things aren’t perfect, that’s all of Earth.”

She finally scoops up the pen. It’s odd – smooth, and there’s text, or something that at least is making an honest attempt to look like text. Right where a brand name should be engraved on the lid. But it’s not. There’s no real letters, just – just squiggles in shapes that letters maybe could make in an alphabet gone slightly to the left.

She blinks and it’s gone, leaving behind plain, unmarred blue plastic. She shrugs it off, and brings it to the page, but before she can even start to write, a 4 appears next to Thomas Morrison’s name.

“Um,” she says. Tries to cross it out. Nothing happens.

The gatekeeper sighs. Again. “Yes?”

“I didn’t –”

“Ah. Apologies, cause and effect should be working properly now.”

“Right,” she says, and this time she can actually scribble out the ‘4’, replace it with a 3.5. The pen behaves itself as she goes through childhood grudges and ex boyfriends and arguments she had in Reddit comment sections. It’s a lot.

“I have a question,” she says, as she rates whether she was attracted to several different individuals, and how she feels about them now.

“I live to serve,” says the clerk.

“How did I die?”

“Drunk driver,” he says. “Not your fault. The funeral was well attended. If you want to see it once you’re set up, someone can track down a recording for you.”

She doesn’t remember it. Doesn’t – where was she before she died? Edinburgh, surely, working on her thesis. Failure points in solar panels. Useful, as she had claimed in her application. But there’s no money in academia. She’s never exactly planned to stay, as she explained herself to her mother. Just to write something.

Still. For all that her life, in hindsight, feels like an exercise in futility, damn whatever bastard decided to jellify her against the roadside.

The clerk pokes at the computer again, as she stands there for a moment. Then she goes back to the form, which appears to have already finished the section she was on and moved on to the next. She clears her throat. No more ink appears.

“So. God’s real?”

“Mmhmm.”

“Evolution?”

“Last I heard, the big guy wishes he came up with it before doing everything by hand.”

“Okay so someone came up with, I don’t know, human genitalia and childhood genetic diseases?” She glances up from the form. “Though I’m sure I’m not the first person to mention the problem of suffering.”

He shrugs. “It’s a reasonable question, though not one with a satisfying answer. I mean, I asked the same thing when I got up here, pretty sure everyone does when they realize it won’t get them kicked out the door.”

“So? What’s the unsatisfying answer?”

“For the genitalia? Extreme jerryrigging. It’s like code; if you take a busy, overworked programmer, obviously you’re going to wind up with an inefficient mess of a solution where everything gets routed together. Can’t sort out temperature control? Guess we’ll just use air to cool the gonads and hope no one decides to kick them.”

He rolls his eyes. “You know, Christianity was 90% right, but they definitely overshot with the whole infallible thing. Plenty of bugs in the code that the big guy’s too lazy to fix.”

“Childhood cancer is a bug in the code?” Alice stares at him. “Not to be Epicurean about it, but that’s – you all seem pretty omnipresent and omnipotent to me, so –”

“Ah well, finite suffering for eternal paradise isn’t the worst trade-off. As a ratio of your total existence, that blip on Earth is infinitesimal, in the most literal sense of the word. It all comes out in the wash.”

“Right,” says Alice, and finds that she dislikes all of this immensely. “I think I will go downstairs, actually, if that’s alright?”

He blinks. “Why?”

She slides the form under the glass and steps back, looking around. The clouds drift in a clockwise circle above her head, though there’s… something about them.

She stares closer. There’s one, the perfect cloud. A normal distribution with lumps in all the right places. A few others, the sorts of clouds made for debates over whether they’re shaped like cows or castles. And then there’s one that’s identical to the first, just reflected over the y-axis and maybe a bit smaller.

Pascal’s Wager. She’s called this asshole’s bluff once already, might as well try what’s already worked once.

“Perhaps I just reject the morality of your system. That’s allowed, isn’t it?”

He stands up, walks out from behind the desk and around to her. Brushes some of his gingery hair out of his face.

“Kiddo, there’s no one else down there. We could arrange some eternal torment, if it’s really what you want, but it’ll take a while to set up and you’ll just be hanging around by yourself for ages. Why not just go on through, we’ll set you up somewhere to live, you’ll see your grandma again. It’ll be perfect.”

“How did I die?” she asks, again. “Because last I remember, I was hosting office hours.”

The desk looks different now.

She squints at it for a second, before it clicks. She couldn’t see her reflection in the glass before. But there she is. And is the computer a different computer?

She blinks. No, it’s the same old white box.

He looks down at her. “Heart attack in your sleep. You wouldn't."

"You said drunk driver." There are, she realizes, four clouds, up to transformation. They're just copies, stretched or shrunk or flipped. "Before, you said it was a drunk driver."

His face goes still for a second, and then he smiles. "Of course. It was traumatic. You wouldn't remember it. Remarkable what the psyche can do to protect itself."

The air suddenly fills with the furious reek of burning rubber, stinging at her nostrils, catching on her palms, on the cuts on her palms as though they’ve skidded over something rough.

She breathes, she tries to breathe but it’s rough and burbling and there’s something wet coming up her throat. Get it out, she needs to get it out, she coughs, but it’s not a cough. Her throat spasm, her lungs hitch but there’s no air, there’s no air there’s nothing coming through she can’t breathe she can’t breathe her heart is shrieking in her useless throat and ears and she can’t

Breathe.

She breathes.

She shakes.

“Like I said,” says the clerk. “The brain doesn’t like to remember trauma.” He holds out a bottle of water that definitely wasn’t in his hand a moment ago. Like the pen, there’s a label on it that could be any of the brands she’s ever seen, but isn’t quite any of them. But she takes it anyway. Drinks. It tastes like water, which is good enough.

Her hand’s shaking, but she’s got to keep her head on straight. “I still want to head downstairs. How long until they’re ready for me?”

He stares at her. The bottle in her hand goes from ribbed, to smooth, back to ribbed again.

“How long?”

“You are aware that you’re signing up for an eternity far worse than what you just experienced?” he asks, flatly.

“Yes.” Does her best to sound confident.

He stares at her. She stares at him. The same four clouds circle overhead. And then he tilts his head, and something sharp sets in behind his eyes. She feels, for a moment, unable to so much as twitch. Like he’s turned her to stone. Then, smoothly he does up a button on his coat, gives a perfect, customer service smile. Bored. Painted on.

“Well, we aim to please. Now, just to be clear, if you go downstairs there’s no coming back up. It’s another one way road.”

“That’s what I assumed. I still want to go.” The water bottle is cool against her hand and she rubs at its ridges. “Now, please.”

He circles back around the desk and sits. “We value informed consent here.”

Her nerves seize all at once. Her legs promptly decide they no longer function as legs and deposit her on the gently glowing linoleum as she spasms, convulses. It’s beyond pain, it’s beyond – her brain, she can feel, repeatedly trying for the off switch but the power stays on.

She twitches over and over in agony that intensifies from impossible to incomprehensible, more than can even be screamed out. The bottle’s gone somewhere, rolled away. She crushed it, maybe, in that first collapse inward.

“It’s been thirty seconds,” says the clerk from the desk. “Halfway through.”

And she lies on that smooth, plastic floor and she suffers.

Passage B:
[Titan, 3713]

She was sweating inside the pressure suit by the time she finished edging her way up the steep hill. Saturn hung overhead, blurred orange by the same atmosphere that had been dragging at her all day. But now she had a moment to catch her breath. She couldn’t see the start of the long descent to Launchpad 23, but the smooth ice of the flat was a far more welcoming prospect than the uneven climb behind her.

She retracted the microspikes along the inside edges of her skis. Nineteen meters per second to fully clear the descent. More than twenty-two and she would risk breaking her leg when the ground flattened out again.

[Interstellar Vessel Flander’s Field, 3822. 27 years of voyage remaining.]

“I was born on Saturn,” the old man tells me. It’s not the first time he’s said it.

He wasn’t old when we boarded, but now he is. Never married, though no one on board ever seemed interested. I’ve never asked why he decided to take the pilgrimage path – perhaps I should have. But I can guess.

“I know,” I say.

“I was the last,” he says, which is also not new. “Everyone dying, and there I was. A baby.” He says it like even he doesn’t believe it. Not really.

“So you’ve said.”

“I was the last,” he repeats.

The doorchime sounds and I open it to let the doctor in. I step out while he does his tests. Take a piss.

He joins me in the corridor after twenty minutes. “You’ll stay with him tonight?” he asks.

“I can,” I say. “Is –”

He shakes his head. “He’s leaving more gently than he came in. You stay with him.”

[L5 Tethys, 3717]

“A word?”

“Maria Callins,” his aide whispered through his earpiece. “Water extraction on Enceladus.”

“M. Callins,” he said.

“Our contract has a buyout clause,” she said, still sitting at the otherwise empty table. No doubt a legacy of burned old earth, back when extraction rights out here were a far lower margin enterprise.

“You’re enforcing it?” he asked.

He’d shown her and the rest of the ‘concerned parties’ the charts. 31.6% of the going rate, under the current contract. All for an operation that had paled beside its sister on Jupiter. In all of their interests, he’d said.

“We’ve upheld our end of the compact. A little consideration would go a long way.” She didn’t smile. She was low-gravity long – shaped by whatever frigid moon gave birth to her.

“We’re freeing you from sales at under a third of what the market would buy your water for,” he said.

“You’re ending a commercial relationship we have taken great pride in maintaining for generations.”

He sat down at the table opposite her, pulling up the chart on the projector again. “Again, this is in all our –”

“And what is your plan for extracting however many bodies you’ve got left down there? We’re all citizens of humanity,” she said, blandly. “I’m a mother, you know?”

There was silence through his earpiece for a second, then, “Maripuso Iceworks. Her daughter married the son last year. Between them, they’re 79% of Saturn-system water production.”

“We’re abiding by our contractual obligations to everyone involved in our proprietary labour solution.”

“You do still have some workers left, don’t you? Because if you’re terminating with us, why, I couldn’t imagine how you’re keeping them hydrated. I know you’re not working with the competi –”

“Fine,” he said.

[Titan, 3713]

Breathing steadied, she shifted her weight forward and pushed into the skate, driving from leg to leg as speed gathered under her. Three meters per second. Five. Eight. Ten. Halfway to the slope now, the ice blurring smooth in the low light. Twelve. Fifteen.

She pushed harder, snapping one ski up before the edge could catch and throw her sideways. Eighteen. Nineteen point three five.

[Interstellar Vessel Flander’s Field, 3801. 48 years of voyage remaining.]

“Don’t stare,” my mother tells me.

“Are you an alien?” I ask, before she can tell me not to.

He’s got two sets of eyelids, the extra one flickering shut as he turns to look into our lit cabin. Doesn’t look human, not even moon-human, long and skinny and always sick. Not like me.

“We’re all aliens,” he says. “Or have you ever been to earth?” He’s smiling when he says it, so he can’t be too upset, but his skin’s shiny like no one I’ve ever seen before.

I shake my head. He’s got an accent that I’ve never heard before, and I used to spend every evening helping my mother out on the docking ports back home. I’ve heard lots of accents.

“I’m from Saturn,” he says. “That’s why I look like this.”

That doesn’t make sense. “I’m from Saturn too,” I say. “We used to live on Enceladus, before –”

“Enough,” my mother says, and pulls me into the cabin, shutting the door.

[Villa Callins, 3713]

Her mother stopped her as she made for bed.

“The shif are closing up shop.”

The words offered up no meaning. Could be some mooner slang from her mother’s youth, could be some corporate acronym she’d just invented. Either way, best to play along. “OK?” she said.

“No more hydrogen extraction. Not here.” Said nice and patronisingly.

“Oh no?” She tried to sidle past her to get to the hallway.

“It puts us in a tricky position – Safia. You could pretend to listen.”

She nodded. “I’m listening. I’m just kind of tired, so – what about – there’s people down there, still, right?”

“They’ll sort them out. What matters is that it further pushes us into an economic corner," her mother said. “And boosts Jupiter even more.”

“Mmhmm,” she said.

“You know Alain Maripuso, don’t you?”

“Sure, I guess. I haven’t spoken to him in ages though.”

“See if he can convince his father to come to stay here. Or in the house on Titan. Say you’ll teach him to ski, or some such.”

“Ok, but Pontmercy hates you, so –”

“So nothing. He benefits just as much as I do from presenting a united front.”

Ah.

But her next race was in under a month, and it would be so very helpful to be down on Titan. “Sure, I’ll get in touch.”

[Callisto, 3800]

“The news this evening: an SPTA team have confirmed that the ‘last man on Saturn’, Callun Connel, has died. Connel, 63, was born on Banach Station in orbit around Jupiter. He was ‘deeply moved’ by news reports from Saturn as a young man, and moved there in 3782, taking the name Zurtir F-1. The SPTA have announced that they will no longer be maintaining the platform on which Connel lived, alongside the few remnants of the mining community.”

[Titan, 3713]

The ridge fell away beneath her. The suit sensed the break and opened wings along her arms and back.

One meter above the ground. Two.

She tilted forward to maintain the arc, thumb hovering over the button for the automated assist. Two-thirds down.

Just beginning to dip below two meters.

She held the angle.

[Callisto, 3726]

“Thirteen years after the Strategic Hydrogen Investment Fund cut shipments to its Saturn hydrogen platforms, the first crewed flights to the atmospheric mining operation since its inception have returned.

“The operation was founded nearly a thousand years ago with a seed population of seven thousand. In late 3713, SHIF records allege their descendants numbered close to half a million.

“Recovery teams have confirmed four hundred and nineteen survivors.

“Yesterday, the unauthorized release of footage taken by the recovery teams has renewed pressure on the Solar Planetary Trade Association to place the Jovian works under direct administration.

“Joining me is Ataraiz M-19, recovered from Saturn with her newborn son, Jatza. Ataraiz, thank you for being here.”

“Hello.”

“And this is your son?”

“Yes.”

“Jatza, is that right?”

“Yes.”

“He is the youngest survivor of the Saturn operation.”

“Yes.”

“You were discharged from hospital only last week. Are you both receiving continuing care?”

“Yes. Jatza still sick. Too thin.”

“There are growing calls now for the SPTA to suspend or revoke SHIF’s remaining hydrogen rights around Jupiter. Have you been following that debate?”

“Don’t know.”

“Of course. Three survivors have reportedly chosen to remain living on one of the mining platforms. What are your thoughts?”

“Is home. I would too, but Jatza.”

“Do you think the Authority has an obligation to maintain the zone for them, despite the cost?”

“Don’t know.”

“Thank you, Ataraiz.”

The cliché of it all is what gets her. The fact that there are literal bloody pearls on the bloody gates, under a perfect blue sky with fluffy clouds floating about. The only thing that doesn’t fit is the desk. It looks like it was ripped from some dentist’s waiting room, glass panels connected to nothing. And a sad looking bloke stuck behind one of three windows. He’s a nondescript little figure, dark brown hair and a black bomber jacket.

“Next,” he says, though there’s no queue, just her. He sounds bored, with an accent she can’t quite place. American.

She steps forward. The floor beneath her shimmers with ethereal light, and squeaks under her trainers.

“Name?”

Screw that. She takes a deep breath. “Is this a dream or a hallucination or… I don’t know – something like that?” Not that she’s ever known she was dreaming before, nor is she prone to hallucinations. Still, it can’t hurt to ask.

“No. You’re dead. No, this isn’t being caused by lack of oxygen to the brain, you’ve made it fully to the other side, and no, you can’t go back. Name?”

“Uh, Alice? Alice B. Clarkson. So is this like – I mean, I wasn’t expecting it to be… Christian.”

He taps away at his all-white box of a computer and squints. “Clarence, Clark, Cl - Clarkson. There you are. Hm. Ok, I’ve got you under atheist, subcategory: pedant. She blinks and it’s gone, leaving behind plain, unmarred blue plastic. She shrugs it off, and brings it to the page, but before she can even start to write, a 4 appears next to Thomas Morrison’s name.

“Um,” she says. Tries to cross it out. Nothing happens.

The gatekeeper sighs. Again. “Yes?”

“I didn’t –”

“Ah. Apologies, cause and effect should be working properly now.”

“Right,” she says, and this time she can actually scribble out the ‘4’, replace it with a 3.5. The pen behaves itself as she goes through childhood grudges and ex boyfriends and arguments she had in Reddit comment sections. It’s a lot.

“I have a question,” she says, as she rates whether she was attracted to several different individuals, and how she feels about them now.

“I live to serve,” says the clerk.

“How did I die?”

“Drunk driver,” he says. “Not your fault. The funeral was well attended. If you want to see it once you’re set up, someone can track down a recording for you.”

She doesn’t remember it. Doesn’t – where was she before she died? Edinburgh, surely, working on her thesis. Failure points in solar panels. Useful, as she had claimed in her application. But there’s no money in academia. She’s never exactly planned to stay, as she explained herself to her mother. Just to write something.

Still. For all that her life, in hindsight, feels like an exercise in futility, damn whatever bastard decided to jellify her against the roadside.

The clerk pokes at the computer again, as she stands there for a moment. Then she goes back to the form, which appears to have already finished the section she was on and moved on to the next. She clears her throat. No more ink appears.

“So. God’s real?”

“Mmhmm.”

“Evolution?”

“Last I heard, the big guy wishes he came up with it before doing everything by hand.”

“Okay so someone came up with, I don’t know, human genitalia and childhood genetic diseases?” She glances up from the form. “Though I’m sure I’m not the first person to mention the problem of suffering.”

He shrugs. “It’s a reasonable question, though not one with a satisfying answer. I mean, I asked the same thing when I got up here, pretty sure everyone does when they realize it won’t get them kicked out the door.”

“So? What’s the unsatisfying answer?”

“For the genitalia? Extreme jerryrigging. It’s like code; if you take a busy, overworked programmer, obviously you’re going to wind up with an inefficient mess of a solution where everything gets routed together. Can’t sort out temperature control? Guess we’ll just use air to cool the gonads and hope no one decides to kick them.”

He rolls his eyes. “You know, Christianity was 90% right, but they definitely overshot with the whole infallible thing. Plenty of bugs in the code that the big guy’s too lazy to fix.”

“Childhood cancer is a bug in the code?” Alice stares at him. “Not to be Epicurean about it, but that’s – you all seem pretty omnipresent and omnipotent to me, so –”

“Ah well, finite suffering for eternal paradise isn’t the worst trade-off. As a ratio of your total existence, that blip on Earth is infinitesimal, in the most literal sense of the word. It all comes out in the wash.”

“Right,” says Alice, and finds that she dislikes all of this immensely. “I think I will go downstairs, actually, if that’s alright?”

He blinks. “Why?”

She slides the form under the glass and steps back, looking around. The clouds drift in a clockwise circle above her head, though there’s… something about them.

She stares closer. There’s one, the perfect cloud. A normal distribution with lumps in all the right places. A few others, the sorts of clouds made for debates over whether they’re shaped like cows or castles. And then there’s one that’s identical to the first, just reflected over the y-axis and maybe a bit smaller.

Pascal’s Wager. She’s called this asshole’s bluff once already, might as well try what’s already worked once.

“Perhaps I just reject the morality of your system. That’s allowed, isn’t it?”

He stands up, walks out from behind the desk and around to her. Brushes some of his gingery hair out of his face.

“Kiddo, there’s no one else down there. We could arrange some eternal torment, if it’s really what you want, but it’ll take a while to set up and you’ll just be hanging around by yourself for ages. Why not just go on through, we’ll set you up somewhere to live, you’ll see your grandma again. It’ll be perfect.”

“How did I die?” she asks, again. “Because last I remember, I was hosting office hours.”

The desk looks different now.

She squints at it for a second, before it clicks. She couldn’t see her reflection in the glass before. But there she is. And is the computer a different computer?

She blinks. No, it’s the same old white box.

He looks down at her. “Heart attack in your sleep. You wouldn't."

"You said drunk driver." There are, she realizes, four clouds, up to transformation. They're just copies, stretched or shrunk or flipped. "Before, you said it was a drunk driver."

His face goes still for a second, and then he smiles. "Of course. It was traumatic. You wouldn't remember it. Remarkable what the psyche can do to protect itself."

The air suddenly fills with the furious reek of burning rubber, stinging at her nostrils, catching on her palms, on the cuts on her palms as though they’ve skidded over something rough.

She breathes, she tries to breathe but it’s rough and burbling and there’s something wet coming up her throat. Get it out, she needs to get it out, she coughs, but it’s not a cough. Her throat spasm, her lungs hitch but there’s no air, there’s no air there’s nothing coming through she can’t breathe she can’t breathe her heart is shrieking in her useless throat and ears and she can’t

Breathe.

She breathes.

She shakes.

“Like I said,” says the clerk. “The brain doesn’t like to remember trauma.” He holds out a bottle of water that definitely wasn’t in his hand a moment ago. Like the pen, there’s a label on it that could be any of the brands she’s ever seen, but isn’t quite any of them. But she takes it anyway. Drinks. It tastes like water, which is good enough.

Her hand’s shaking, but she’s got to keep her head on straight. “I still want to head downstairs. How long until they’re ready for me?”

He stares at her. The bottle in her hand goes from ribbed, to smooth, back to ribbed again.

“How long?”

“You are aware that you’re signing up for an eternity far worse than what you just experienced?” he asks, flatly.

“Yes.” Does her best to sound confident.

He stares at her. She stares at him. The same four clouds circle overhead. And then he tilts his head, and something sharp sets in behind his eyes. She feels, for a moment, unable to so much as twitch. Like he’s turned her to stone. Then, smoothly he does up a button on his coat, gives a perfect, customer service smile. Bored. Painted on.

“Well, we aim to please. Now, just to be clear, if you go downstairs there’s no coming back up. It’s another one way road.”

“That’s what I assumed. I still want to go.” The water bottle is cool against her hand and she rubs at its ridges. “Now, please.”

He circles back around the desk and sits. “We value informed consent here.”

Her nerves seize all at once. Her legs promptly decide they no longer function as legs and deposit her on the gently glowing linoleum as she spasms, convulses. It’s beyond pain, it’s beyond – her brain, she can feel, repeatedly trying for the off switch but the power stays on.

She twitches over and over in agony that intensifies from impossible to incomprehensible, more than can even be screamed out. The bottle’s gone somewhere, rolled away. She crushed it, maybe, in that first collapse inward.

“It’s been thirty seconds,” says the clerk from the desk. “Halfway through.”

And she lies on that smooth, plastic floor and she suffers.

I'd like your view on two passages.

For this comparison, please read both passages carefully before making your choice.

Passage A:
There is a box of lychees sitting pretty next to his doormat. Half empty already, with a note on top. He bends down and picks up the paper – very familiar handwriting, though it’s much more legible than her physics homework tends to be. He still hasn’t looked at those mock exams of hers; he’ll have to do it tonight before bed.

‘Mum got these organic and they’re going off – thought you might enjoy! x Lydia’.

He smiles. That’s very kind of them. And Miranda splashed out for organic. European, even! What a luxury. And it saves him a trip to the shop. His smile fades a little once he picks up the fruit, which are definitely on the turn. Sagging, with skin browned and bruised. No mould, of course, Miranda’s a bit of an obsessive there, but still far from appetizing. But the intention was generous, and besides, he’s got a use for them. He scoops them up.

Pressing his thumb to the scanner, he heads into his flat and straight into the kitchen, where he grabs a plate from the cupboard and tips the fruit out onto it. Tweezers, he needs tweezers. None in his pocket, of course there aren’t. He grabs some from the bathroom, before returning to the unappealing mound. He picks one up, turns it around, sets it aside. Continues. Until – there: he reaches in and plucks a dead insect off the side of a fruit. Oxygen deprivation before it was packed, nothing chemical. That’s the organic promise!

He places the bug on a saucer and keeps going. By the end, he has eight little bodies on his late grandmother’s fine china, all in a row. He should take them now, but – oh, a moment of self indulgence won’t make a difference. The Europeans are clearly less aggressive in their cleaning, this is much better pickings than he gets from his usual grocer but they’ll have cost at least thirty percent more. He squints at the plate. Five ants, those he finds frequently; two white larval things, which he doesn’t think are maggots, though what would he know; and what surely must be a caterpillar. That’s a first. He taps the table to turn it on.

“Black and yellow fuzzy caterpillar. Small.”

Leanne’s voice chirps in. “It seems that you’re trying to find information about caterpillars. Caterpillars are the larval stage of butterflies, and historically were found wherever butterflies were –”

“Skip,” he instructs. “Just tell me about small black and yellow fuzzy caterpillars. What species?”

It buffers for a second. “That sounds like it might be a small tortoiseshell caterpillar. They were the national butterfly of Denmark, and used to live throughout Eurasia. They used to feed on nettles, before the soil preservation act of –”

“End.” He turns off the table.

Once the screen’s dark again, he takes a moment with the caterpillar, turns it around in the tweezers. It’s less colourful in real life than it looked in Leanne’s generated model. Still. Remarkable. It joins the others.

He glances at the fruit. Perhaps he should have one, if only so that when he next runs into Lydia and Miranda in the hall, he can truthfully say that they were eaten. But then he’d be lying and saying they were tasty, and the whole knot would only get more tangled. He leaves them there instead, and takes his small collection of insects through to his home office.

When he toured this apartment six months ago, the property manager had all but locked him in this room, begging him to appreciate the floor to ceiling windows, the speaker system, the modern aircon. The pitch had worked; he’d moved in two weeks later. Now it’s warm, airless and dark. Blackout blinds keep out the evening sun, every crack or hole is sealed up, save one, and the sound system has not been used in months. He opens the door quickly and shuts it behind himself again just as fast. Winces at the currents it stirs up.

“Buddy?” he calls. Gives his eyes a second to adjust before scanning the walls. Bare – the door must have scared him. He switches on the dimmed light before bending down to check the crack between the built-in corkboard and the ledge. A few dark legs draw themselves even tighter in. “There you are. Got you some dinner – well, technically Lydia did.” He begins placing the dead insects into the gap. “I’ve told you about her, the girl down the hall? My student? Used to have our lessons in here, maybe you saw her then. Between you and me, she’s not getting her A, but don’t tell her mother that or I’ll be out of a job.”

He empties the plate, and settles down onto the bare floor. Keeps his eyes fixed on the space and doesn’t move an inch. Seconds drag on. Minutes. And then the small, dark shape begins to shift itself. He holds his breath. It darts forward through its narrow channel to the dead insects.

“There,” he says, without quite meaning to. A brief pause, but the small jerks and spasms of feeding time continue as he watches. It’s hard to tell just which of his offerings are tonight’s meal, not unless he were to shine a torch in there, but that would be far too invasive. But by the time Buddy shifts back, there’s still plenty of indistinguishable insectoid lumps left. That’s good, that’s a store. One of Buddy’s hairy legs briefly flicks out from under the board as he moves himself around, presumably settling himself down for a nap.

It is a shame he’s not doing it out on the board. There’s a sketchpad on the rarely used desk that he’s filled with drawings of the low flat body, the eight splayed legs. He’s a handsome spider, is his Buddy. But apparently one who has decided that today he’ll be doing his best impression of a slightly spiky dark blob.

He stands. Ten years ago, he’d have hunched for hours but time, ah. Never enough of it. It’ll be a new century in a few months, first time in a hundred years!

Less caution is needed in leaving. Buddy’s hidden away where he feels safest, there’s no real worry about scaring him. He’ll stay there for a while now with no need to hunt. Back out to the kitchen to feed himself. Not with the lychees, he’s got Greek left from Tuesday. He reheats it and eats, as the fruit stare at him from the counter.

Once he’s done, meal finished and tidied, they’re still at it. Two can play at that game – he looks right back at them. He doesn’t want them. And he rather doubts that Buddy does either. He picks one up, the firm skin yielding under the slightest pressure. Maybe he could finally become his mother, stick them in sugar water in a can. The sort of sweet treat that they used to eat in heatwaves.

The fruit lands back on the plate with a heavy squelch. It bursts open on impact, flesh spilling out from a slit running up and down the brown. He shudders. Even though he knows that he was only touching its skin, he still wipes his hand on his napkin. It smells sickly sweet, far worse than he would have expected it to when it was all held in. It’s the sort of smell that would have sent his mother into a frenzy of bagging up everything sugary, wiping down every surface for fear of attracting ‘bugs’.

No risk of that these days. Not even then. Sure, they were technically rural, but he was six when the hygiene laws were passed and there hadn’t been agriculture in the area for, god, thirty years? But she was never so vindicated as the one summer the neighbours had roaches and had to ring up the bureau and have the whole place sealed up for a week. And when they came round to check on his childhood home, there was not one to be found.

He’ll decide what to do with the lychees later.

He fishes Lydia’s mock exam out of his bag. Her writing is characteristically illegible, she’s lost a quarter of the marks to the grader not being able to read her damn work. But she clearly has been paying attention in their sessions – got her acceleration-velocity-time triangle all in order. So that’s something. Progress.

Dawn comes, as it does, while he’s halfway to the bus stop. Already he’s pre-empting it out the door, soon he’ll be arriving at school before the sun shows up. But so it goes, so it goes. He pauses right before scanning on; he forgot to bin the fruit. Could turn back, be late. But he’s got a class second period, his year nine, no time for that. A day won’t make a difference, he’ll just air out the room later. Instead he slinks to his usual seat, past the usual faces who share this daily pilgrimage. They’re all far too used to each other to bother acknowledging it.

The day goes. His older students are worried about exams, his younger students about the promise of future exams, and all of them are desperately trying to show that they don’t care. He’s never quite clear on if he used to be able to connect with them. Definitely, he used to be more invested. But there are teachers who can ‘chat’. Who joke with their classes. He’s sure he’s never been quite able to do that.

Buddy needs more food, so he heads to the local grocer in the evening, his usual organic supplier. Ryan’s there today, for the first time in a few weeks. She waves him over.

“How’re things?” she asks.

He nods. “I haven’t seen you?”

“Ah,” she says, leaning against the counter. He waits for her to continue. “I told you about my mother?”

He’s not sure. “No.”

“She’s sick,” says Ryan. “And my sister’s being useless, so I’ve been looking after her. It’s a whole mess.”

He glances at the aisles back. But he’s in this conversation now. “I’m sorry.”

“Ah, well. Your parents still around?”

He shakes his head.

She copies him. “Sorry to hear that. My dad died a few years back, the old bastard.”

He’s misinterpreted, he realizes. But explaining that feels fraught. “My mother never left Birmingham,” he says instead, since that could mean anything. “I don’t go back there much.”

She smiles. “You don’t miss home? I mean, you’re always in here by yourself. No partner? No kids?”

He could explain it to her. She’s probably fifteen years younger than him, no sense of that world he was born in. He’s given Lydia the same speech — Gen Z, Gen Alpha. Then the last generation. None of them planned on children. Of course he became a teacher. Of course Miranda needs to succeed as a mother. But Ryan seems desperate for a chat, unlike twelve year old Lydia who’d wanted nothing less than to consider her mother’s personhood. They’d be stuck on that for hours, and he’s no desire to be psychoanalysed by his grocer. So instead he says, “I didn’t really want that. I should get on?”

She smiles again. “Sure.”

He rushes off towards the back room. Turns briefly. She’s there, at the checkout counter by herself. This shop is perfectly busy plenty of the time, it’s just late and it’s near closing and it’s just random chance that he’s the only one here. But.

Anyway. He brushes past the shelves of locally grown hydroponics to the rather pricier Californian origin organic ‘produce’. Though compared to the French-grown lychees, it’s probably borderline affordable.

The fruit is meant to be in boxes. This section is meant to have shelves, stacked up with plastic tubs, the very ones that the fruit was in when the all natural insecticide was applied. Sixteen quid for a box of strawberries, or twenty dollars. Though Ryan always kicks up a fuss if people don’t use pounds, despite what GBUS says.

The point isn’t that. The point is that the fruit does not come in bins. It has never before been sold like that, by the gram, where he’d have to dig through mounds of the stuff to try to find anything useful while everyone watched – while everyone – the – he’s not doing anything illegal, he just – this isn’t what he comes here for.

Ryan has followed him. “Need some help?” she asks.

“No - it’s - you’ve changed the layout.” His voice cracks. “Why have you changed the layout?”

“New rules for imported groceries."

“What do you mean?” he asks.

She crosses over to join him at the back of the shop. “The Americans said the Aussies were ‘spreading pests’, so now everything coming in has to be checked individually. It’s a bloody nightmare, completely messing with my shipments. And customs are charging an arm and a leg for the privilege of bruising my apples. God bless bureaucracy.”

This is – oh no. “But this stuff’s from the States?”

“Dunno what to tell you,” she says. “It’s this Renew lot, they lobbied to make it all imports including from the US.”

“Why?” He knows. Of course he does. The decouple movement, the Euro-nationalists, there’s plenty they can get done when they agree. But they weren’t meant to do something like this.

He looks into the bins of perfectly clean fruit. “It’s everything?”

She sighs. “Look, if you’re worried about the cost hikes, the local stuff’s not impacted at all.”

“It’s not about the money, it’s –” He could tell her. About Buddy, about how hard it is finding anything he can eat. But – Buddy’s not a bee, or a butterfly, or Miranda and Lydia’s hyper-allergenic cat. “I just don’t like the way hydroponics tastes. It’s bland.”

“Then what’s the problem?” She grabs an apple from the top of the tub of pink ladies and sticks it in his hand. “Try it. On me. They can’t wash out flavour, promise.”

He nods. “Of course.”

No point in buying anything, so he doesn’t. He eats his apple on the way home and tries not to panic. There are other shops, there are other options. He can figure something out. Surely.

Once, he read that London was the most surveilled city in the world. If it were ever true, it isn’t now. Hasn’t been for sixty-odd years. But sometimes he feels like there are eyes everywhere, looking for any sign that he’s not right, not normal. Not happy. There’s CCTV on the front of his apartment building, in the lift and the staircase, in case he wanted to avoid it that way, in the hall. His doorbell’s a camera, so’s everyone else’s. The company who made his access scanner had a class action lawsuit six months ago for selling customer data. The whole world is watching him go home. But inside – oh, inside is his. He can drop the apple core on the floor and face no consequences for littering, he can lean his head against the wall and yell and have no one rubberneck or pretend to care. He can go into Buddy’s room and sit there quietly until he comes out and crawls up and down the corkboard in search of something that isn’t coming back.

Passage B:
“Most people have many memories of their mothers. I flatter myself by asserting that I have more. A lifetime of claustrophobically close proximity, as we circled Great Britain. We have lived every moment together – every teenage argument, every moment of grief or joy. I struggle to think of any memory where my mother is not there.

“But when I think of her, I always remember a throwaway comment some twenty years ago. Of course, I am no longer the child of back then, trying to get her attention as she stared at a sunset while we pulled out of Fort William. The sky was always at its best when leaving, she told me. It didn’t make much sense at the time, since we always seemed to be leaving somewhere, but I think the adult that I am now understands a little better.”

Charlotte fumbled for her water glass and took a sip. There was more on the page, the litany of thanks, a string of stupid anecdotes that she found she couldn’t bear the thought of saying. Fuck it all. She set down the cup, spilling a few drops onto the paper.

“May the sky be beautiful for her now, too.”

“Hear, hear!”

She wasn’t sure who said it, but it was enough of an excuse to dip her head and step away. To take the shovel and tip dirt onto her mother’s casket. Her aunt did the same, then that was all the family done and they could all shuffle back towards the fleet of cabs waiting to take them to the station.

They loaded up onto the reception car, which had been set up while they’d been out. She found herself by Maggie, handing out cups of over-milked tea to a crowd which was two thirds fellow passengers and one third random family friends she’d met maybe once in her life. They all knew who she was, of course.

“She was a great woman,” said someone-or-other. “I am so, so sorry for your loss.”

She handed him a cup of tea. “Thank you.”

“So.” Bertie leaned up against the table. “Will the Countess Denham be taking her mother’s seat in the Lords?”

She shoved some tea into his hands. “You just want someone to entertain you.”

“Not an answer, my dear.”

Under them, the train sagged before pulling itself into motion. The passengers barely moved. She reached out to steady the table before the mugs could fall off.

“Imo will have my head if I don’t.” She glanced up, trying to work out where the Baroness of Hexham had gotten to. There – a grey-streaked head bobbing in the midst of a crowd down the far end of the carriage. “It’s something to do, I suppose.”

“What a patriotic way to think about it. Now come. You can’t hide over here all afternoon.”

“I’m hardly hiding!” she protested, but let him pull her into the crowd anyway.

Fucking condolences. A mob of grievers and well-wishers, a parliament in black, pecking at her skin with their half-baked stories about a woman who couldn’t give a damn about any of them, even on the rare occasions that she managed to pull herself out of her own head and notice that there was a world around her. But that was the speech that she chucked out of the window a hundred miles ago – ‘No one was more disappointed by my mother than me. Now she’s dead. God damn it.’ That would have shut them all up.

“Lottie!” Ah, shit. “Oh, dear girl.” Imo grabbed her arm and pulled her into her huddle.

They all looked at her. Half people she’d known all her life, half strangers, all staring at her with their stupid, faux-sad eyes. She did her best to school her face into an appropriate expression of grief.

“Oh, my dear,” said Imo again, patting at her shoulder. “What a hard day it has been for all of us. But you’re bearing up so admirably.”

She nodded, dutifully.

“Have you met my cousins?” she asked.

Charlotte had. Probably. She dug back through a poorly stacked heap of memories of times they’d stopped in Northumberland. “Of course,” she said. “William and Michael Percy. Thank you both for coming. It’d mean a lot to her to know you were here.”

“Of course,” said the one on the left. “She was a great woman.”

She’d hated the Percy family. Hated anyone who’d managed to hold onto their great houses, whose family trusts had emerged any more intact than her own. But let her peers call her a ‘great woman’, let her Wikipedia article declare her the eighth Marquess of Denham and have very little else to say, and let the rest of the world continue on happily without ever concerning itself over her existence.

“I know.”

They stood there for a moment in utter, awkward silence – made infinitely worse by the chatter that bounced up and down the rest of the carriage.

“You know,” said the one on the right, “Michael was actually talking to Imo about joining you all for a few years.”

“Oh?” said Charlotte, grateful for the conversation starter, and to have learned which was Michael and which William.

“It just seems rather an adventure,” said Michael.

“Oh, it’s wonderful.” Imo patted her shoulder. “Wouldn’t you agree, Lottie?”

“Such an adventure,” she agreed.

“I mean, I understand the role of the high speed network but really this does just seem like a much more civilized mode of travel. The two hardly have anything in common.” He glanced upwards out of the window, to where the HS5 track made its way through the sky. “You just can’t see anything from up there. No, if you really want to learn a place, you must travel it slowly. Your eulogy reminded me of that, you know?”

“It did?” asked Charlotte.

“You have to be somewhere to leave it. Properly be somewhere, not zip by.”


[]


“Order!” Imo smacked her hammer against her gavel. There was no notable change in the quiet conversations dotting the room, but she seemed satisfied enough and sat down.

Charlotte leaned over to Bertie. “Is she pretending to be a judge?”

“She believes it lends her noble Ladyship gravitas,” he whispered back.

Charlotte considered that for a second, then shrugged.

“Bet I can set them all off,” he said, grinning like an arse when she glanced at him.

“The floor is now open for questions,” said Imo.

Bertie stood. “My Lords, good afternoon. Once again I find myself obliged to raise the question of the luncheon menu. May I ask whether the noble Lord, the Minister for the Kitchens, might enlighten the House as to when we may expect some new options?”

A chorus of ‘Hear, hear!’ rose up. On the other side of the carriage, Horace McWilliams, Earl of Glencairne, stood. “My Lords, I thank the noble Lord for raising this matter for the sixth sitting in succession. As I informed your Lordships last week, discussions with the kitchen staff are ongoing, and I shall of course report to the House when there is any development.”

“No one likes the lasagna, my Lords!” someone called from the benches.

“My Lords, I am aware that—”

“So change it!”

Another wave of voices rang out as Bertie sat smugly down beside her.

“They’ve been talking about this for five weeks?” she called out, raising her voice over the hubbub.

“Eleven, my Lady!” he shouted back. “I only joined in a month ago.”

The train jolted as it rolled round a corner, and the mace slid from the table in front of Imo. She rose, retrieved it with great dignity, and set it back in its place before sinking down again, her head in her hands.

Eventually she grabbed her hammer again, and smacked it back against the gavel. “Enough!”

The lords took back to their benches, though not without a considerable amount of glaring across the train aisle.

“My Lords, the only business before the House is the Second Reading of the House of Lords Abolition Bill, as brought from the Commons in the year of our Lord 2063, and resubmitted annually thereafter. I call upon the noble Lord, the Earl of Rochester.”

Rochester rose. “My Lords, I fear that once again we gather in dutiful repetition, as we have done each Session for the past forty years, to consider whether we ought to abolish ourselves. Your Lordships will recall that last Session, and the Session before that, and indeed every Session preceding those, we resolved that, however desirable our abolition might appear in principle, the practicalities rendered it most inconvenient.”

The mace fell again. Imo stared at it, and didn’t move. “My Lords, the Question is that the House of Lords Abolition Bill be read a Second time. As many as are of that opinion say ‘Content’.”

Bertie, next to her, said, “Content.” No one else did.

“Of the contrary, ‘Not Content’.”

A much louder chorus chimed up in response. Charlotte said nothing. There did not seem to be much point.

The clerk stood. “Contents, 1. Not-Contents, 97. So the Not-Contents have it.”

“The Bill is, accordingly, rejected. Business being concluded, the House stands adjourned until tomorrow, when we shall resume with the same Bill.”

Everyone stood and shuffled off towards the dining car. “Is that it?” asked Charlotte.

Bertie shrugged. “Imo clearly wasn’t on form today. A shame – usually there’s much more fighting.”
