Passage B:
“We are?”
My hands are wrapped around something smooth and warm. I rub my thumb over it until I find a tiny divot – too small to dream. But there. Real.
I open my eyes. She’s kneeling in front of me. She leans in, clasping her hands around mine on the mug.
Steam dampens my chin.
She smiles. “That we are.”
I want to touch her cheek, but I don’t want to break contact. I lean forward instead and bump our foreheads before retreating.
“That was a long one,” she says. “North again?”
I shake my head and stand, my legs protesting the movement. She’s unsteady too. “Were you here the whole time?”
“Only after I got you tea,” she says.
It’s hot enough to itch at my palms – she can’t have been kneeling for long.
“We’ll have guests soon.”
“Your soon or my soon?” she asks.
I consider the dream. Father Sun sets behind one eye, while Mother Sun rises behind the other. “Now.”
“Drink your tea,” she says.
I’m still holding the mug, I realize – haven’t dropped it or drunk from it or – she taps the rim.
“Drink.”
I sip. In the dream it was mint. This is the first of the verbena – it tastes of its planting and plucking and dying and drying, but mostly of lemon. “It’s good.”
“Guests?” she prompts.
“For me,” I say. I open the door to the sharp sunlight. We stand in our little corner of desert-edge. As I look south, I see a ship carving around the dunes, no doubt to the port at Landsmeet. She’s looking at it too.
She doesn’t see our guests, though I do. Sixty degrees of Father Sun’s descent, trekking to the first green. Half a season, the way everdark Rest counts it. The heat. The sand. The woman in front: unknown, armed, angry. Thief, purrs the dream. The blurred lines of time and place, as I-we-he followed-will have followed him-her. Them and us, them and –
She presses her fingers into my pulse point. Sharp. Not quite painful, but enough to drag me back from then and into now. Our guests are here. Two men, not two women; not us. Thin and ragged, with more journeying to come.
“Which of you is the prophet?” the lordling asks. He could be any dusty wanderer, except for the faintly glowing oath burned into his arm. It curls around his bicep, calls him here and calls him back the way he came.
She lets me step forward. “It’s already too late,” I tell them. “That’s no bad thing.”
The lordling’s lips twist. “It’s not.”
I sigh. “He already has an oracle to ignore; why bother a prophet? But fine, here is your answer: he pulls the trap shut around himself. Cryptic enough?” I can’t keep the amused crinkle from my eyes. How I have missed riddling.
“I swore I’d find you,” he says. Holds out his arm. “No one in the capital has any answers; my father said  ”
“This is what I know: by the time you return, you will have a new king. There is nothing I can tell you that would change that.”
She stiffens. No harm in it, though. There really is nothing they can do; I wouldn’t have dreamed it otherwise.
“I promised I’d bring you back. for the sake of your people, won’t you –”
“Not our people,” she says. Measured. She’s watching his companion, who stands behind him with the sharpness of a knife.
Perhaps she’s right. It doesn’t matter, anyway. I shake my head. “Come. Let us shelter you from the sun.”
“No swords.” She tightens her grip.
The lordling obeys. So does the other one, though I’ve no doubt he still has edges that can cut. And then she lets them inside.
“It must be strange,” he says. “It’s so – primitive.” He looks like he regrets the last word even as he says it.
“The light is gentler here.” I widen the gap in the shutters to allow a little more in, as she helps them offload their packs.
“But you’ve no power, no –”
“No sewers,” she says. “There’s a hut out back.”
She sits them down and pours them cups of whey.
“No water treatment either?” asks the knife. The first thing he’s said, edged with humour.
She scoff-laughs.
The boy sips and bravely doesn’t make a face. “We won’t force you. But –”
	“No,” she says.
He means it, is the thing.
“But you’d have hot showers and lights and –”
I cross over to join them. “Every luxury. But no. We are happy here.”
She relaxes. I do mean it. She should know that. I won’t leave here until the time for dreams is done, and when I do, we won’t be going south.
We feed them, and let them take the bed. I make her up a nest on the ground, but don’t join her. I don’t want to go too deep into dream right now. I go to watch the sand, set to orange by the sun – only a handful of degrees until Sunswap, now.
The knife is behind me, though he thinks I haven’t noticed.
“Did we know each other?” I ask. I watch their journey back, I watch his little lord arrive  alone.
“I was Aisker’s man when he hosted you at Dawnwatch.”
“Hm.” I wonder what he thinks now, if he still sees the half-sane creature I was then before she plucked me away to this place where I am more woman than dream. “And why are you here?”
“To protect his son.”
I say nothing.
“He wants you back.”
There’s the cutting edge, then. “Are you going to drag me back across the desert?” I ask. He could try, I suppose, though it surely won’t end happily.
“I’m meant to,” he says. “She’s the one who stole you?”
“If I am my own, then I give myself to her,” I say.
He leans on the balcony next to me. “If you’re right, I’m not sure anyone will care if I bring you back or not.”
“On this, I am.”
Now he’s silent, but I have the advantage – I know he’s about to speak.
“I’m glad you’ve found this,” he says.
His decision sets, and the dream sets with it. I dig a nail into a small crack in the wood. “If you were wise, you’d head north.” Pointless, I know.
“Does he make it home?”
“If you’re with him.”
“Then I’ll go with him.”
If I did want to go with them, to go back, would she let me? Would she follow? I won’t ask.
They do stay till Sunswap in the end. Even follow us up to Landsmeet. I watch them, as Father Sun reddens one horizon and Mother Sun pinks the other. It’s their first time meeting people who aren’t from Rest and aren’t sailors, and it’s been a long time since Dawnwatch was a port.
It seems to delight them. Music that still sounds otherworldly to me, even after half a lifetime of hearing it. The nomads’ curd cheeses, their whey brew that burns the throat and leaves the little lord asleep well before the green flash. It’s a shame – his only chance to see it. When it comes, it makes his companion jump, which makes me laugh into her neck. Even she smiles a bit. One sun sinks beneath the horizon, the other starts its climb.
They come to me one more time before they leave.
“No,” I tell them, before they can start.
“My father –” begins the lordling.
“Has nothing to offer me,” I tell him. “I have given him enough.” I shake my head, then look at his knife. “You could still go north.”
“You could still go south,” he says, and smiles. It’s freer now than the half-thing that he arrived with.
“No.” She says it with me.
The little lord looks like he wants to say something, but instead turns away. His oath sears itself into his flesh. Unfulfilled, it brands him with his choice.
They leave. The lordling to home, his knife to whatever happens to keep him from that home.
She leans against me, and I press a kiss to the side of her head.
“We’ll be done with the dream,” I tell her. “And we’ll go north to the end of the world where the suns go in circles around the horizon and people will think we’re mad when we tell them of the desert.”
“When?” she asks.
“Soon.”
“Your soon, or mine?”
I look South. Not hers, that’s for sure. The dream still twists through its turns. But it’ll be sooner than suits the man who I see stumbling alone into his father’s hall, even as he starts the journey that will bring him there. But that’s alright – it’s a far-off thing now. Our part is done.
“Something in between, I think.” I smile at her. “Time enough for a few more dreams.”
“Hm. I’ll put the kettle on.”
I follow her inside.

Passage B:
“Most people have many memories of their mothers. I flatter myself by asserting that I have more. A lifetime of claustrophobically close proximity, as we circled Great Britain. We have lived every moment together – every teenage argument, every moment of grief or joy. I struggle to think of any memory where my mother is not there.

“But when I think of her, I always remember a throwaway comment some twenty years ago. Of course, I am no longer the child of back then, trying to get her attention as she stared at a sunset while we pulled out of Fort William. The sky was always at its best when leaving, she told me. It didn’t make much sense at the time, since we always seemed to be leaving somewhere, but I think the adult that I am now understands a little better.”

Charlotte fumbled for her water glass and took a sip. There was more on the page, the litany of thanks, a string of stupid anecdotes that she found she couldn’t bear the thought of saying. Fuck it all. She set down the cup, spilling a few drops onto the paper.

“May the sky be beautiful for her now, too.”

“Hear, hear!”

She wasn’t sure who said it, but it was enough of an excuse to dip her head and step away. To take the shovel and tip dirt onto her mother’s casket. Her aunt did the same, then that was all the family done and they could all shuffle back towards the fleet of cabs waiting to take them to the station.

They loaded up onto the reception car, which had been set up while they’d been out. She found herself by Maggie, handing out cups of over-milked tea to a crowd which was two thirds fellow passengers and one third random family friends she’d met maybe once in her life. They all knew who she was, of course.

“She was a great woman,” said someone-or-other. “I am so, so sorry for your loss.”

She handed him a cup of tea. “Thank you.”

“So.” Bertie leaned up against the table. “Will the Countess Denham be taking her mother’s seat in the Lords?”

She shoved some tea into his hands. “You just want someone to entertain you.”

“Not an answer, my dear.”

Under them, the train sagged before pulling itself into motion. The passengers barely moved. She reached out to steady the table before the mugs could fall off.

“Imo will have my head if I don’t.” She glanced up, trying to work out where the Baroness of Hexham had gotten to. There – a grey-streaked head bobbing in the midst of a crowd down the far end of the carriage. “It’s something to do, I suppose.”

“What a patriotic way to think about it. Now come. You can’t hide over here all afternoon.”

“I’m hardly hiding!” she protested, but let him pull her into the crowd anyway.

Fucking condolences. A mob of grievers and well-wishers, a parliament in black, pecking at her skin with their half-baked stories about a woman who couldn’t give a damn about any of them, even on the rare occasions that she managed to pull herself out of her own head and notice that there was a world around her. But that was the speech that she chucked out of the window a hundred miles ago – ‘No one was more disappointed by my mother than me. Now she’s dead. God damn it.’ That would have shut them all up.

“Lottie!” Ah, shit. “Oh, dear girl.” Imo grabbed her arm and pulled her into her huddle.

They all looked at her. Half people she’d known all her life, half strangers, all staring at her with their stupid, faux-sad eyes. She did her best to school her face into an appropriate expression of grief.

“Oh, my dear,” said Imo again, patting at her shoulder. “What a hard day it has been for all of us. But you’re bearing up so admirably.”

She nodded, dutifully.

“Have you met my cousins?” she asked.

Charlotte had. Probably. She dug back through a poorly stacked heap of memories of times they’d stopped in Northumberland. “Of course,” she said. “William and Michael Percy. Thank you both for coming. It’d mean a lot to her to know you were here.”

“Of course,” said the one on the left. “She was a great woman.”

She’d hated the Percy family. Hated anyone who’d managed to hold onto their great houses, whose family trusts had emerged any more intact than her own. But let her peers call her a ‘great woman’, let her Wikipedia article declare her the eighth Marquess of Denham and have very little else to say, and let the rest of the world continue on happily without ever concerning itself over her existence.

“I know.”

They stood there for a moment in utter, awkward silence – made infinitely worse by the chatter that bounced up and down the rest of the carriage.

“You know,” said the one on the right, “Michael was actually talking to Imo about joining you all for a few years.”

“Oh?” said Charlotte, grateful for the conversation starter, and to have learned which was Michael and which William.

“It just seems rather an adventure,” said Michael.

“Oh, it’s wonderful.” Imo patted her shoulder. “Wouldn’t you agree, Lottie?”

“Such an adventure,” she agreed.

“I mean, I understand the role of the high speed network but really this does just seem like a much more civilized mode of travel. The two hardly have anything in common.” He glanced upwards out of the window, to where the HS5 track made its way through the sky. “You just can’t see anything from up there. No, if you really want to learn a place, you must travel it slowly. Your eulogy reminded me of that, you know?”

“It did?” asked Charlotte.

“You have to be somewhere to leave it. Properly be somewhere, not zip by.”


[]


“Order!” Imo smacked her hammer against her gavel. There was no notable change in the quiet conversations dotting the room, but she seemed satisfied enough and sat down.

Charlotte leaned over to Bertie. “Is she pretending to be a judge?”

“She believes it lends her noble Ladyship gravitas,” he whispered back.

Charlotte considered that for a second, then shrugged.

“Bet I can set them all off,” he said, grinning like an arse when she glanced at him.

“The floor is now open for questions,” said Imo.

Bertie stood. “My Lords, good afternoon. Once again I find myself obliged to raise the question of the luncheon menu. May I ask whether the noble Lord, the Minister for the Kitchens, might enlighten the House as to when we may expect some new options?”

A chorus of ‘Hear, hear!’ rose up. On the other side of the carriage, Horace McWilliams, Earl of Glencairne, stood. “My Lords, I thank the noble Lord for raising this matter for the sixth sitting in succession. As I informed your Lordships last week, discussions with the kitchen staff are ongoing, and I shall of course report to the House when there is any development.”

“No one likes the lasagna, my Lords!” someone called from the benches.

“My Lords, I am aware that—”

“So change it!”

Another wave of voices rang out as Bertie sat smugly down beside her.

“They’ve been talking about this for five weeks?” she called out, raising her voice over the hubbub.

“Eleven, my Lady!” he shouted back. “I only joined in a month ago.”

The train jolted as it rolled round a corner, and the mace slid from the table in front of Imo. She rose, retrieved it with great dignity, and set it back in its place before sinking down again, her head in her hands.

Eventually she grabbed her hammer again, and smacked it back against the gavel. “Enough!”

The lords took back to their benches, though not without a considerable amount of glaring across the train aisle.

“My Lords, the only business before the House is the Second Reading of the House of Lords Abolition Bill, as brought from the Commons in the year of our Lord 2063, and resubmitted annually thereafter. I call upon the noble Lord, the Earl of Rochester.”

Rochester rose. “My Lords, I fear that once again we gather in dutiful repetition, as we have done each Session for the past forty years, to consider whether we ought to abolish ourselves. Your Lordships will recall that last Session, and the Session before that, and indeed every Session preceding those, we resolved that, however desirable our abolition might appear in principle, the practicalities rendered it most inconvenient.”

The mace fell again. Imo stared at it, and didn’t move. “My Lords, the Question is that the House of Lords Abolition Bill be read a Second time. As many as are of that opinion say ‘Content’.”

Bertie, next to her, said, “Content.” No one else did.

“Of the contrary, ‘Not Content’.”

A much louder chorus chimed up in response. Charlotte said nothing. There did not seem to be much point.

The clerk stood. “Contents, 1. Not-Contents, 97. So the Not-Contents have it.”

“The Bill is, accordingly, rejected. Business being concluded, the House stands adjourned until tomorrow, when we shall resume with the same Bill.”

Everyone stood and shuffled off towards the dining car. “Is that it?” asked Charlotte.

Bertie shrugged. “Imo clearly wasn’t on form today. A shame – usually there’s much more fighting.”

Passage B:
Six p.m. on a Friday, and you’re still in your office. Door shut, staring blankly at a computer screen. I wasn’t planning to start off too heavy on the symbolism, but why would you choose to spend your life in a windowless box? It’s the destination, why d’you gotta make it the journey as well?

It’s a bad day for it, too. The sort of day where any sane person would be outside, enjoying the evening air and spending time with other people. Normal people. Interesting people. People who could enrich your life, bring meaning to your muddle, give you the gift of variety beyond the tunnel-vision world that you occupy. But you. You strange, strange, str-str-str-strange thing that you are, you’d rather be there breathing in the chalk dust and staring fruitlessly at a paper. You’re not going to understand it, you do realize? You’ve been staring at it for four hours, maybe five - even I’m not sure at this point - and you’re still not sure what an isolated type is or how in the hell you wound up doing model theory. I mean, you are many things but a model theorist is /not/ one of them. Close the document, I beg of thee.

Of course, you won’t do that. There might be something useful in there, some new way to look at the latest problem you’ve set yourself. After all, your qual is coming up. The big day. The biggest of days. You’re going to have to stand there in front of (gasp) your advisor and your almost-advisor-but-that-one-academic-match-making-meeting-was-kind-of-awkward and some guy from Lie Groups that you dragged in because you did a course at one point and it was the only thing you could think of for your minor topic.

You have to be right where you are. You have to be studying away, with all the diligence of the damned. Buried before you’re dead, except instead of a coffin it’s your office and instead of earth piling up atop you it’s a mountain of definitions you don’t remember and instead of a priest it’s your advisor asking you a question and you stare at her blankly because you do not for the life of you remember what any of those words mean and -

Oh. You’re panicking. Oh dear.

Don’t worry. I’m sure you’ll be fine. Lots of people fail their -

Well. A few people fail their quals. It’s not the end of the world.

Though you’ve never met anyone who failed their qual, have you? Maybe they just won’t admit to it. Shame. Humiliation, even. The unlucky 1%, the only 1% you’ve any chance of making it into you aspiring academic, you.

But you’ll be fi-i-ine. You’ve got a syllabus. Cribbed from a list your advisor sent you, questions some other student of hers you’ve never met presumably survived. How, you have no idea. Because you’ve never heard of half the things on here, even though you d e f initely should have, and you’ve been avoiding learning the other half because they sound scary. But hey, you’ll always have Lie groups.

You’ve got to focus, you tell yourself. You spin in your chair to look at your chalkboard, at the practice problems you’ve hunted-and-gathered from the weird-n-wild corners of math.overflow, to the weirder-n-wilder corners of the brains of your academic siblings. Of the ten you’ve got, you’ve managed to solve two and both of those were rather like pulling teeth.

You sigh and run your hand down your face. This is hopeless. You’re hopeless. You’ll never get anywhere at this rate. No, this calls for some outside intervention.

Do you:

A) Reach out to your advisor - she’ll set the questions, maybe if you look pathetic enough, she’ll give you hints about what you ought to focus on. But you’ll be exposing your soft, squishy belly like the desperate little pup you are.

B) Email the student who’s syllabus you’re using. He’s still listed as a student at the school, when you google him, though you’ve never spoken to him. Honestly, you’re pretty sure you’ve never even seen him. But he passed the exam using this syllabus. He might be able to identify the key ideas.

C) Beg your academic siblings for help. You’re all in this together, right? They might not be able to help, and suffering shared might not be suffering divided, but at least they’ll be suffering too. If all else fails, you can see if they’ll pity-comp your dinner.

D) Surely there’s something in this model theory paper that can help. Or at least something your committee doesn’t know - when in doubt, apply surface level understanding of something completely unrelated. Confusion is always your friend (apart from when it’s your enemy).

“But when I think of her, I always remember a throwaway comment some twenty years ago. Of course, I am no longer the child of back then, trying to get her attention as she stared at a sunset while we pulled out of Fort William. The sky was always at its best when leaving, she told me. It didn’t make much sense at the time, since we always seemed to be leaving somewhere, but I think the adult that I am now understands a little better.”

Charlotte fumbled for her water glass and took a sip. There was more on the page, the litany of thanks, a string of stupid anecdotes that she found she couldn’t bear the thought of saying. Fuck it all. She set down the cup, spilling a few drops onto the paper.

“May the sky be beautiful for her now, too.”

“Hear, hear!”

She wasn’t sure who said it, but it was enough of an excuse to dip her head and step away. To take the shovel and tip dirt onto her mother’s casket. Her aunt did the same, then that was all the family done and they could all shuffle back towards the fleet of cabs waiting to take them to the station.

They loaded up onto the reception car, which had been set up while they’d been out. She found herself by Maggie, handing out cups of over-milked tea to a crowd which was two thirds fellow passengers and one third random family friends she’d met maybe once in her life. They all knew who she was, of course.

“She was a great woman,” said someone-or-other. “I am so, so sorry for your loss.”

She handed him a cup of tea. “Thank you.”

“So.” Bertie leaned up against the table. “Will the Countess Denham be taking her mother’s seat in the Lords?”

She shoved some tea into his hands. “You just want someone to entertain you.”

“Not an answer, my dear.”

Under them, the train sagged before pulling itself into motion. The passengers barely moved. She reached out to steady the table before the mugs could fall off.

“Imo will have my head if I don’t.” She glanced up, trying to work out where the Baroness of Hexham had gotten to. There – a grey-streaked head bobbing in the midst of a crowd down the far end of the carriage. “It’s something to do, I suppose.”

“What a patriotic way to think about it. Now come. You can’t hide over here all afternoon.”

“I’m hardly hiding!” she protested, but let him pull her into the crowd anyway.

Fucking condolences. A mob of grievers and well-wishers, a parliament in black, pecking at her skin with their half-baked stories about a woman who couldn’t give a damn about any of them, even on the rare occasions that she managed to pull herself out of her own head and notice that there was a world around her. But that was the speech that she chucked out of the window a hundred miles ago – ‘No one was more disappointed by my mother than me. Now she’s dead. God damn it.’ That would have shut them all up.

“Lottie!” Ah, shit. “Oh, dear girl.” Imo grabbed her arm and pulled her into her huddle.

They all looked at her. Half people she’d known all her life, half strangers, all staring at her with their stupid, faux-sad eyes. She did her best to school her face into an appropriate expression of grief.

“Oh, my dear,” said Imo again, patting at her shoulder. “What a hard day it has been for all of us. But you’re bearing up so admirably.”

She nodded, dutifully.

“Have you met my cousins?” she asked.

Charlotte had. Probably. She dug back through a poorly stacked heap of memories of times they’d stopped in Northumberland. “Of course,” she said. “William and Michael Percy. Thank you both for coming. It’d mean a lot to her to know you were here.”

“Of course,” said the one on the left. “She was a great woman.”

She’d hated the Percy family. Hated anyone who’d managed to hold onto their great houses, whose family trusts had emerged any more intact than her own. But let her peers call her a ‘great woman’, let her Wikipedia article declare her the eighth Marquess of Denham and have very little else to say, and let the rest of the world continue on happily without ever concerning itself over her existence.

“I know.”

They stood there for a moment in utter, awkward silence – made infinitely worse by the chatter that bounced up and down the rest of the carriage.

“You know,” said the one on the right, “Michael was actually talking to Imo about joining you all for a few years.”

“Oh?” said Charlotte, grateful for the conversation starter, and to have learned which was Michael and which William.

“It just seems rather an adventure,” said Michael.

“Oh, it’s wonderful.” Imo patted her shoulder. “Wouldn’t you agree, Lottie?”

“Such an adventure,” she agreed.

“I mean, I understand the role of the high speed network but really this does just seem like a much more civilized mode of travel. The two hardly have anything in common.” He glanced upwards out of the window, to where the HS5 track made its way through the sky. “You just can’t see anything from up there. No, if you really want to learn a place, you must travel it slowly. Your eulogy reminded me of that, you know?”

“It did?” asked Charlotte.

“You have to be somewhere to leave it. Properly be somewhere, not zip by.”

“Order!” Imo smacked her hammer against her gavel. There was no notable change in the quiet conversations dotting the room, but she seemed satisfied enough and sat down.

Charlotte leaned over to Bertie. “Is she pretending to be a judge?”

“She believes it lends her noble Ladyship gravitas,” he whispered back.

Charlotte considered that for a second, then shrugged.

“Bet I can set them all off,” he said, grinning like an arse when she glanced at him.

“The floor is now open for questions,” said Imo.

Bertie stood. “My Lords, good afternoon. Once again I find myself obliged to raise the question of the luncheon menu. May I ask whether the noble Lord, the Minister for the Kitchens, might enlighten the House as to when we may expect some new options?”

A chorus of ‘Hear, hear!’ rose up. On the other side of the carriage, Horace McWilliams, Earl of Glencairne, stood. “My Lords, I thank the noble Lord for raising this matter for the sixth sitting in succession. As I informed your Lordships last week, discussions with the kitchen staff are ongoing, and I shall of course report to the House when there is any development.”

“No one likes the lasagna, my Lords!” someone called from the benches.

“My Lords, I am aware that—”

“So change it!”

Another wave of voices rang out as Bertie sat smugly down beside her.

“They’ve been talking about this for five weeks?” she called out, raising her voice over the hubbub.

“Eleven, my Lady!” he shouted back. “I only joined in a month ago.”

The train jolted as it rolled round a corner, and the mace slid from the table in front of Imo. She rose, retrieved it with great dignity, and set it back in its place before sinking down again, her head in her hands.

Eventually she grabbed her hammer again, and smacked it back against the gavel. “Enough!”

The lords took back to their benches, though not without a considerable amount of glaring across the train aisle.

“My Lords, the only business before the House is the Second Reading of the House of Lords Abolition Bill, as brought from the Commons in the year of our Lord 2063, and resubmitted annually thereafter. I call upon the noble Lord, the Earl of Rochester.”

Rochester rose. “My Lords, I fear that once again we gather in dutiful repetition, as we have done each Session for the past forty years, to consider whether we ought to abolish ourselves. Your Lordships will recall that last Session, and the Session before that, and indeed every Session preceding those, we resolved that, however desirable our abolition might appear in principle, the practicalities rendered it most inconvenient.”

The mace fell again. Imo stared at it, and didn’t move. “My Lords, the Question is that the House of Lords Abolition Bill be read a Second time. As many as are of that opinion say ‘Content’.”

Bertie, next to her, said, “Content.” No one else did.

“Of the contrary, ‘Not Content’.”

A much louder chorus chimed up in response. Charlotte said nothing. There did not seem to be much point.

The clerk stood. “Contents, 1. Not-Contents, 97. So the Not-Contents have it.”

“The Bill is, accordingly, rejected. Business being concluded, the House stands adjourned until tomorrow, when we shall resume with the same Bill.”

Everyone stood and shuffled off towards the dining car. “Is that it?” asked Charlotte.

Bertie shrugged. “Imo clearly wasn’t on form today. A shame – usually there’s much more fighting.”

Passage B:
I got as far as Norway. The first plane out of Newark in the right direction took me to Oslo, which was at least closer to Finland than New York. Perhaps there was some greater hand steering my purpose, that saw the sleeper train up to Trondheim still running on Christmas Eve. Every inch fought northward was a battle, but one the universe seemed to want me to win. Until it didn’t.

We got past Lillehammer before everything ground to a halt. We had a cabin to ourselves, me lying there uselessly with the oxygen tank on the floor next to my bed and Arnie on the top bunk listening to me wheeze away. Good reason to raise hopeless children – if they never manage to find someone willing to marry them, they can follow you north to watch you die.

He swung himself off the bunk and opened the blind. I pushed myself up on my elbows so I could see out – nothing. The odd juddering lantern light, white on the white of the snow, as the staff rushed back and forth along the length of the stopped train.

"The heating's still on," said Arnie, hand over the vent. "Can't be anything too wrong."

He shifted his weight from foot to foot, still standing by the little sink looking out the window.

I wheezed at him for lack of any other response.

"Should I go ask what's going on?" he asked.

"What's that going to help?"

"They could tell us when we'll be moving again?"

High rising terminal. Again. Useless boy. But there was no point in him being here.

"Go on then," I said.

He dithered for a moment, fiddling with the settings on the heating until I waved him away.

“Go.”

I lay back as the door slid open then closed again.

Was that my breathing, or the wind? Both.

Of course he’d come early.

Had he been up there since the train stopped, or had he only arrived once Arnie left? Didn't matter much. He slid his legs over the edge, just like Arnie had done, and down off the bunk. In green, now, wrapped in furs the colour of the forest I caught the edge of as we landed. Smelled like pine and snow and something raw and mammalian. Primitive. Outside, one of the lanterns caught its light on the window, capturing a black-and-white moment of all that picture imperfect snow, and there in front of it: him. His hat. That marketing-ready red that I’d put on him.

"I was going after you," I said.

He leaned over me, staring. I knew what he saw. Withered. Collapsed inward by the long years since I created him out of the bastardized pieces of a million myths and set him on the world to ruin me – career, marriage, et al. He, of course, hadn't aged; he was as old as he'd always been. A polite fiction that mocked the ravages of time.

"I was going to kill you,” I told him. “But the Norwegians, god, what a stupid, smug people. Wouldn’t sell me a gun. Thought the Finns might be more helpful.”

He wheezed at me, slow and mocking. It wasn’t quite like my breathing, more like the wind as it sucked itself in between and under the carriages of the train. And like the snow, the white ball at the end of his hat fell limply on my shoulder and I didn't mean to do it, God, but I flinched away and he wheezed again. He leaned down and placed his teeth around my throat, pinning me down like a dog proving dominance. They were cold and animal sharp and pressed into every juddering breath I took, but he didn't bite down. I felt a tremor start somewhere in me, until I was all shaking, and still he didn’t bite down. After a long minute, he pulled back and stared down at me.

Oh, god, how he hated me. What a thing to be hated by.

"Do it, then, you bastard. Kill me. I had reindeer for dinner last night. Dry and bland, and I ate every single bite."

He reached out with one calloused, cold-burned finger, and sketched a cross on my mouth below the cannula. It left a trail of something wet and, when I licked my lips, familiarly sweet.

"Don't you dare," I said. He turned to go, and I flung myself out of the bunk, hit the ground, tubes yanking but holding. "I don't need your forgiveness," I tried to shout, though I'd knocked the air out of myself so there was no force behind it. "I don’t forgive you! You’ve had my life, you bastard, you don’t get the high ground here. Kill me or I’ll kill you!"

That got him to stop. There was red bleeding from his hat, dripping down the hollows of his cheeks and pooling on his shoulders. He swelled as I looked at him, filling out the furs even as they hardened into unbroken, velvet red.

Year after year after year, drawing him into being until we were both two bitter old men with smiles painted on our faces.

"Wasn’t even my idea," I said. "I just made you famous. Should be thanking me. I’ll find your fucking wife, how’s that for turnabout?"

He reached behind him, and then set something at the foot of the bed before walking out and leaving me there on the floor. I didn’t try to follow; the chase had escaped me. Heaved myself back onto my bed and readjusted the oxygen before I needed to take a moment to feel dizzy. Then I opened the box he left and took the bottle out and let it fall from my hand against the metal of the frame, let it shatter and spill.

Haven’t seen a glass one for years. But it's been a long time since I've had a Coke.

***

When he opens the door to the cabin, the air tastes of the sticky-sweet of spilled soda. Then he spots the bits of broken glass, the bottom of the bottle and the top and the scattered pieces of the middle and he rushes in. Finally, finally, he sees his pop. Lying there, arm hanging off the bed like he's pointing to where it's fallen.

"Dad?" he asks, and picks his way over to him.

Nothing. Too much nothing, just the faint hissing of the heating still fighting the hold of the endless snow, almost drowned out by the much louder sibilance of the wind, and the occasional shout from outside. And then the oxygen tank gets to screaming at him and he blinks at it stupidly before the leaflets from the doctor overtake his brain.

He grabs him by his shoulder and rolls him onto his back. He goes limply, the cannula crooked in his nose, his eyes open and staring. No pulse.

Here’s a thing: he knows, in theory, how to do CPR. Staying alive, staying alive, press his lips to the old bastard’s shrivelled slugs and see if it takes.

But he doesn’t want to. Too much of him feels like he can finally breathe, he doesn’t want to share that air with anyone right now. So instead he slides those glassy peepers shut. It’s squishier than it looks in the movies, and he's not sure why he does it, other than that it's a thing one probably ought to do. Then he turns off the machine.

All of a sudden, he feels profoundly orphaned, more than he thought he would. He’ll have to find a way back to Oslo, book a flight home, ring his sister and mother to give them the news, even if they haven’t spoken to the old man in decades.

He spots a small box at the foot of the bed. Shiny and red, with a green bow stuck on the lid. He picks it up, and turns it about in his hands. Nothing – empty, no note tucked inside. That earns a frown. Maybe the train staff, bringing a drink around to apologize for the delay? But surely he’d have caught them at it as he was going up and down the train.

He puts it down, and crosses to the still uncovered window. His foot sticks briefly in the drying drink, still slowly staining the carpet as it spreads. It's perfectly dark, though his brief foray outside told him that it's still snowing. He goes to pull the blind down, to give the old man the semblance of privacy before he goes to find someone who looks like they probably ought to be informed that there's a – that – what has happened.

And then, in the brief swinging of a lantern as one of the engineers makes their way towards the front of the train, he sees a man out in the distance.

All in red, standing at the edge of the light, looking towards the train. He falls back into shadow for a second and Arnie blinks, not sure if he’s seeing things. The lamp catches him again. He’s in dark green now, though he’s holding something red. Small and limp, with bits of white. He drops it in the snow before the engineer passes him completely, and though Arnie squints, there’s no way to tell which shadow could be him.

All in red, standing at the edge of the light, looking towards the train. He falls back into shadow for a second and Arnie blinks, not sure if he’s seeing things. The lamp catches him again. He’s in dark green now, though he’s holding something red. Small and limp, with bits of white. He drops it in the snow before the engineer passes him completely, and though Arnie squints, there’s no way to tell which shadow could be him.

Passage B:
“Most people have many memories of their mothers. I flatter myself by asserting that I have more. A lifetime of claustrophobically close proximity, as we circled Great Britain. We have lived every moment together – every teenage argument, every moment of grief or joy. I struggle to think of any memory where my mother is not there.

“But when I think of her, I always remember a throwaway comment some twenty years ago. Of course, I am no longer the child of back then, trying to get her attention as she stared at a sunset while we pulled out of Fort William. The sky was always at its best when leaving, she told me. It didn’t make much sense at the time, since we always seemed to be leaving somewhere, but I think the adult that I am now understands a little better.”

Charlotte fumbled for her water glass and took a sip. There was more on the page, the litany of thanks, a string of stupid anecdotes that she found she couldn’t bear the thought of saying. Fuck it all. She set down the cup, spilling a few drops onto the paper.

“May the sky be beautiful for her now, too.”

“Hear, hear!”

She wasn’t sure who said it, but it was enough of an excuse to dip her head and step away. To take the shovel and tip dirt onto her mother’s casket. Her aunt did the same, then that was all the family done and they could all shuffle back towards the fleet of cabs waiting to take them to the station.

They loaded up onto the reception car, which had been set up while they’d been out. She found herself by Maggie, handing out cups of over-milked tea to a crowd which was two thirds fellow passengers and one third random family friends she’d met maybe once in her life. They all knew who she was, of course.

“She was a great woman,” said someone-or-other. “I am so, so sorry for your loss.”

She handed him a cup of tea. “Thank you.”

“So.” Bertie leaned up against the table. “Will the Countess Denham be taking her mother’s seat in the Lords?”

She shoved some tea into his hands. “You just want someone to entertain you.”

“Not an answer, my dear.”

Under them, the train sagged before pulling itself into motion. The passengers barely moved. She reached out to steady the table before the mugs could fall off.

“Imo will have my head if I don’t.” She glanced up, trying to work out where the Baroness of Hexham had gotten to. There – a grey-streaked head bobbing in the midst of a crowd down the far end of the carriage. “It’s something to do, I suppose.”

“What a patriotic way to think about it. Now come. You can’t hide over here all afternoon.”

“I’m hardly hiding!” she protested, but let him pull her into the crowd anyway.

Fucking condolences. A mob of grievers and well-wishers, a parliament in black, pecking at her skin with their half-baked stories about a woman who couldn’t give a damn about any of them, even on the rare occasions that she managed to pull herself out of her own head and notice that there was a world around her. But that was the speech that she chucked out of the window a hundred miles ago – ‘No one was more disappointed by my mother than me. Now she’s dead. God damn it.’ That would have shut them all up.

“Lottie!” Ah, shit. “Oh, dear girl.” Imo grabbed her arm and pulled her into her huddle.

They all looked at her. Half people she’d known all her life, half strangers, all staring at her with their stupid, faux-sad eyes. She did her best to school her face into an appropriate expression of grief.

“Oh, my dear,” said Imo again, patting at her shoulder. “What a hard day it has been for all of us. But you’re bearing up so admirably.”

She nodded, dutifully.

“Have you met my cousins?” she asked.

Charlotte had. Probably. She dug back through a poorly stacked heap of memories of times they’d stopped in Northumberland. “Of course,” she said. “William and Michael Percy. Thank you both for coming. It’d mean a lot to her to know you were here.”

“Of course,” said the one on the left. “She was a great woman.”

She’d hated the Percy family. Hated anyone who’d managed to hold onto their great houses, whose family trusts had emerged any more intact than her own. But let her peers call her a ‘great woman’, let her Wikipedia article declare her the eighth Marquess of Denham and have very little else to say, and let the rest of the world continue on happily without ever concerning itself over her existence.

“I know.”

They stood there for a moment in utter, awkward silence – made infinitely worse by the chatter that bounced up and down the rest of the carriage.

“You know,” said the one on the right, “Michael was actually talking to Imo about joining you all for a few years.”

“Oh?” said Charlotte, grateful for the conversation starter, and to have learned which was Michael and which William.

“It just seems rather an adventure,” said Michael.

“Oh, it’s wonderful.” Imo patted her shoulder. “Wouldn’t you agree, Lottie?”

“Such an adventure,” she agreed.

“I mean, I understand the role of the high speed network but really this does just seem like a much more civilized mode of travel. The two hardly have anything in common.” He glanced upwards out of the window, to where the HS5 track made its way through the sky. “You just can’t see anything from up there. No, if you really want to learn a place, you must travel it slowly. Your eulogy reminded me of that, you know?”

“It did?” asked Charlotte.

“You have to be somewhere to leave it. Properly be somewhere, not zip by.”


[]


“Order!” Imo smacked her hammer against her gavel. There was no notable change in the quiet conversations dotting the room, but she seemed satisfied enough and sat down.

Charlotte leaned over to Bertie. “Is she pretending to be a judge?”

“She believes it lends her noble Ladyship gravitas,” he whispered back.

Charlotte considered that for a second, then shrugged.

“Bet I can set them all off,” he said, grinning like an arse when she glanced at him.

“The floor is now open for questions,” said Imo.

Bertie stood. “My Lords, good afternoon. Once again I find myself obliged to raise the question of the luncheon menu. May I ask whether the noble Lord, the Minister for the Kitchens, might enlighten the House as to when we may expect some new options?”

A chorus of ‘Hear, hear!’ rose up. On the other side of the carriage, Horace McWilliams, Earl of Glencairne, stood. “My Lords, I thank the noble Lord for raising this matter for the sixth sitting in succession. As I informed your Lordships last week, discussions with the kitchen staff are ongoing, and I shall of course report to the House when there is any development.”

“No one likes the lasagna, my Lords!” someone called from the benches.

“My Lords, I am aware that—”

“So change it!”

Another wave of voices rang out as Bertie sat smugly down beside her.

“They’ve been talking about this for five weeks?” she called out, raising her voice over the hubbub.

“Eleven, my Lady!” he shouted back. “I only joined in a month ago.”

The train jolted as it rolled round a corner, and the mace slid from the table in front of Imo. She rose, retrieved it with great dignity, and set it back in its place before sinking down again, her head in her hands.

Eventually she grabbed her hammer again, and smacked it back against the gavel. “Enough!”

The lords took back to their benches, though not without a considerable amount of glaring across the train aisle.

“My Lords, the only business before the House is the Second Reading of the House of Lords Abolition Bill, as brought from the Commons in the year of our Lord 2063, and resubmitted annually thereafter. I call upon the noble Lord, the Earl of Rochester.”

Rochester rose. “My Lords, I fear that once again we gather in dutiful repetition, as we have done each Session for the past forty years, to consider whether we ought to abolish ourselves. Your Lordships will recall that last Session, and the Session before that, and indeed every Session preceding those, we resolved that, however desirable our abolition might appear in principle, the practicalities rendered it most inconvenient.”

The mace fell again. Imo stared at it, and didn’t move. “My Lords, the Question is that the House of Lords Abolition Bill be read a Second time. As many as are of that opinion say ‘Content’.”

Bertie, next to her, said, “Content.” No one else did.

“Of the contrary, ‘Not Content’.”

A much louder chorus chimed up in response. Charlotte said nothing. There did not seem to be much point.

The clerk stood. “Contents, 1. Not-Contents, 97. So the Not-Contents have it.”

“The Bill is, accordingly, rejected. Business being concluded, the House stands adjourned until tomorrow, when we shall resume with the same Bill.”

Everyone stood and shuffled off towards the dining car. “Is that it?” asked Charlotte.

Bertie shrugged. “Imo clearly wasn’t on form today. A shame – usually there’s much more fighting.”

[Titan, 3713]

She was sweating inside the pressure suit by the time she finished edging her way up the steep hill. Saturn hung overhead, blurred orange by the same atmosphere that had been dragging at her all day. But now she had a moment to catch her breath. She couldn’t see the start of the long descent to Launchpad 23, but the smooth ice of the flat was a far more welcoming prospect than the uneven climb behind her.

She retracted the microspikes along the inside edges of her skis. Nineteen meters per second to fully clear the descent. More than twenty-two and she would risk breaking her leg when the ground flattened out again.

[Interstellar Vessel Flander’s Field, 3822. 27 years of voyage remaining.]

“I was born on Saturn,” the old man tells me. It’s not the first time he’s said it.

He wasn’t old when we boarded, but now he is. Never married, though no one on board ever seemed interested. I’ve never asked why he decided to take the pilgrimage path – perhaps I should have. But I can guess.

“I know,” I say.

“I was the last,” he says, which is also not new. “Everyone dying, and there I was. A baby.” He says it like even he doesn’t believe it. Not really.

“So you’ve said.”

“I was the last,” he repeats.

The doorchime sounds and I open it to let the doctor in. I step out while he does his tests. Take a piss.

He joins me in the corridor after twenty minutes. “You’ll stay with him tonight?” he asks.

“I can,” I say. “Is –”

He shakes his head. “He’s leaving more gently than he came in. You stay with him.”

[L5 Tethys, 3717]

“A word?”

“Maria Callins,” his aide whispered through his earpiece. “Water extraction on Enceladus.”

“M. Callins,” he said.

“Our contract has a buyout clause,” she said, still sitting at the otherwise empty table. No doubt a legacy of burned old earth, back when extraction rights out here were a far lower margin enterprise.

“You’re enforcing it?” he asked.

He’d shown her and the rest of the ‘concerned parties’ the charts. 31.6% of the going rate, under the current contract. All for an operation that had paled beside its sister on Jupiter. In all of their interests, he’d said.

“We’ve upheld our end of the compact. A little consideration would go a long way.” She didn’t smile. She was low-gravity long – shaped by whatever frigid moon gave birth to her.

“We’re freeing you from sales at under a third of what the market would buy your water for,” he said.

“You’re ending a commercial relationship we have taken great pride in maintaining for generations.”

He sat down at the table opposite her, pulling up the chart on the projector again. “Again, this is in all our –”

“And what is your plan for extracting however many bodies you’ve got left down there? We’re all citizens of humanity,” she said, blandly. “I’m a mother, you know?”

There was silence through his earpiece for a second, then, “Maripuso Iceworks. Her daughter married the son last year. Between them, they’re 79% of Saturn-system water production.”

“We’re abiding by our contractual obligations to everyone involved in our proprietary labour solution.”

“You do still have some workers left, don’t you? Because if you’re terminating with us, why, I couldn’t imagine how you’re keeping them hydrated. I know you’re not working with the competi –”

“Fine,” he said.

[Titan, 3713]

Breathing steadied, she shifted her weight forward and pushed into the skate, driving from leg to leg as speed gathered under her. Three meters per second. Five. Eight. Ten. Halfway to the slope now, the ice blurring smooth in the low light. Twelve. Fifteen.

She pushed harder, snapping one ski up before the edge could catch and throw her sideways. Eighteen. Nineteen point three five.

[Interstellar Vessel Flander’s Field, 3801. 48 years of voyage remaining.]

“Don’t stare,” my mother tells me.

“Are you an alien?” I ask, before she can tell me not to.

He’s got two sets of eyelids, the extra one flickering shut as he turns to look into our lit cabin. Doesn’t look human, not even moon-human, long and skinny and always sick. Not like me.

“We’re all aliens,” he says. “Or have you ever been to earth?” He’s smiling when he says it, so he can’t be too upset, but his skin’s shiny like no one I’ve ever seen before.

I shake my head. He’s got an accent that I’ve never heard before, and I used to spend every evening helping my mother out on the docking ports back home. I’ve heard lots of accents.

“I’m from Saturn,” he says. “That’s why I look like this.”

That doesn’t make sense. “I’m from Saturn too,” I say. “We used to live on Enceladus, before –”

“Enough,” my mother says, and pulls me into the cabin, shutting the door.

[Villa Callins, 3713]

Her mother stopped her as she made for bed.

“The shif are closing up shop.”

The words offered up no meaning. Could be some mooner slang from her mother’s youth, could be some corporate acronym she’d just invented. Either way, best to play along. “OK?” she said.

“No more hydrogen extraction. Not here.” Said nice and patronisingly.

“Oh no?” She tried to sidle past her to get to the hallway.

“It puts us in a tricky position – Safia. You could pretend to listen.”

She nodded. “I’m listening. I’m just kind of tired, so – what about – there’s people down there, still, right?”

“They’ll sort them out. What matters is that it further pushes us into an economic corner," her mother said. “And boosts Jupiter even more.”

“Mmhmm,” she said.

“You know Alain Maripuso, don’t you?”

“Sure, I guess. I haven’t spoken to him in ages though.”

“See if he can convince his father to come to stay here. Or in the house on Titan. Say you’ll teach him to ski, or some such.”

“Ok, but Pontmercy hates you, so –”

“So nothing. He benefits just as much as I do from presenting a united front.”

Ah.

But her next race was in under a month, and it would be so very helpful to be down on Titan. “Sure, I’ll get in touch.”

[Callisto, 3800]

“The news this evening: an SPTA team have confirmed that the ‘last man on Saturn’, Callun Connel, has died. Connel, 63, was born on Banach Station in orbit around Jupiter. He was ‘deeply moved’ by news reports from Saturn as a young man, and moved there in 3782, taking the name Zurtir F-1. The SPTA have announced that they will no longer be maintaining the platform on which Connel lived, alongside the few remnants of the mining community.”

[Titan, 3713]

The ridge fell away beneath her. The suit sensed the break and opened wings along her arms and back.

One meter above the ground. Two.

She tilted forward to maintain the arc, thumb hovering over the button for the automated assist. Two-thirds down.

Just beginning to dip below two meters.

She held the angle.

[Callisto, 3726]

“Thirteen years after the Strategic Hydrogen Investment Fund cut shipments to its Saturn hydrogen platforms, the first crewed flights to the atmospheric mining operation since its inception have returned.

“The operation was founded nearly a thousand years ago with a seed population of seven thousand. In late 3713, SHIF records allege their descendants numbered close to half a million.

“Recovery teams have confirmed four hundred and nineteen survivors.

“Yesterday, the unauthorized release of footage taken by the recovery teams has renewed pressure on the Solar Planetary Trade Association to place the Jovian works under direct administration.

“Joining me is Ataraiz M-19, recovered from Saturn with her newborn son, Jatza. Ataraiz, thank you for being here.”

“Hello.”

“And this is your son?”

“Yes.”

“Jatza, is that right?”

“Yes.”

“He is the youngest survivor of the Saturn operation.”

“Yes.”

“You were discharged from hospital only last week. Are you both receiving continuing care?”

“Yes. Jatza still sick. Too thin.”

“There are growing calls now for the SPTA to suspend or revoke SHIF’s remaining hydrogen rights around Jupiter. Have you been following that debate?”

“Don’t know.”

“Of course. Three survivors have reportedly chosen to remain living on one of the mining platforms. What are your thoughts?”

“Is home. I would too, but Jatza.”

“Do you think the Authority has an obligation to maintain the zone for them, despite the cost?”

“Don’t know.”

“Thank you, Ataraiz.”

She was sweating inside the pressure suit by the time she finished edging her way up the steep hill. Saturn hung overhead, blurred orange by the same atmosphere that had been dragging at her all day. But now she had a moment to catch her breath. She couldn’t see the start of the long descent to Launchpad 23, but the smooth ice of the flat was a far more welcoming prospect than the uneven climb behind her.

She retracted the microspikes along the inside edges of her skis. Nineteen meters per second to fully clear the descent. More than twenty-two and she would risk breaking her leg when the ground flattened out again.

[Interstellar Vessel Flander’s Field, 3822. 27 years of voyage remaining.]

“I was born on Saturn,” the old man tells me. It’s not the first time he’s said it.

He wasn’t old when we boarded, but now he is. Never married, though no one on board ever seemed interested. I’ve never asked why he decided to take the pilgrimage path – perhaps I should have. But I can guess.

“I know,” I say.

“I was the last,” he says, which is also not new. “Everyone dying, and there I was. A baby.” He says it like even he doesn’t believe it. Not really.

“So you’ve said.”

“I was the last,” he repeats.

The doorchime sounds and I open it to let the doctor in. I step out while he does his tests. Take a piss.

He joins me in the corridor after twenty minutes. “You’ll stay with him tonight?” he asks.

“I can,” I say. “Is –”

He shakes his head. “He’s leaving more gently than he came in. You stay with him.”

[L5 Tethys, 3717]

“A word?”

“Maria Callins,” his aide whispered through his earpiece. “Water extraction on Enceladus.”

“M. Callins,” he said.

“Our contract has a buyout clause,” she said, still sitting at the otherwise empty table. No doubt a legacy of burned old earth, back when extraction rights out here were a far lower margin enterprise.

“You’re enforcing it?” he asked.

He’d shown her and the rest of the ‘concerned parties’ the charts. 31.6% of the going rate, under the current contract. All for an operation that had paled beside its sister on Jupiter. In all of their interests, he’d said.

“We’ve upheld our end of the compact. A little consideration would go a long way.” She didn’t smile. She was low-gravity long – shaped by whatever frigid moon gave birth to her.

“We’re freeing you from sales at under a third of what the market would buy your water for,” he said.

“You’re ending a commercial relationship we have taken great pride in maintaining for generations.”

He sat down at the table opposite her, pulling up the chart on the projector again. “Again, this is in all our –”

“And what is your plan for extracting however many bodies you’ve got left down there? We’re all citizens of humanity,” she said, blandly. “I’m a mother, you know?”

There was silence through his earpiece for a second, then, “Maripuso Iceworks. Her daughter married the son last year. Between them, they’re 79% of Saturn-system water production.”

“We’re abiding by our contractual obligations to everyone involved in our proprietary labour solution.”

“You do still have some workers left, don’t you? Because if you’re terminating with us, why, I couldn’t imagine how you’re keeping them hydrated. I know you’re not working with the competi –”

“Fine,” he said.

[Titan, 3713]

Breathing steadied, she shifted her weight forward and pushed into the skate, driving from leg to leg as speed gathered under her. Three meters per second. Five. Eight. Ten. Halfway to the slope now, the ice blurring smooth in the low light. Twelve. Fifteen.

She pushed harder, snapping one ski up before the edge could catch and throw her sideways. Eighteen. Nineteen point three five.

[Interstellar Vessel Flander’s Field, 3801. 48 years of voyage remaining.]

“Don’t stare,” my mother tells me.

“Are you an alien?” I ask, before she can tell me not to.

He’s got two sets of eyelids, the extra one flickering shut as he turns to look into our lit cabin. Doesn’t look human, not even moon-human, long and skinny and always sick. Not like me.

“We’re all aliens,” he says. “Or have you ever been to earth?” He’s smiling when he says it, so he can’t be too upset, but his skin’s shiny like no one I’ve ever seen before.

I shake my head. He’s got an accent that I’ve never heard before, and I used to spend every evening helping my mother out on the docking ports back home. I’ve heard lots of accents.

“I’m from Saturn,” he says. “That’s why I look like this.”

That doesn’t make sense. “I’m from Saturn too,” I say. “We used to live on Enceladus, before –”

“Enough,” my mother says, and pulls me into the cabin, shutting the door.

[Villa Callins, 3713]

Her mother stopped her as she made for bed.

“The shif are closing up shop.”

The words offered up no meaning. Could be some mooner slang from her mother’s youth, could be some corporate acronym she’d just invented. Either way, best to play along. “OK?” she said.

“No more hydrogen extraction. Not here.” Said nice and patronisingly.

“Oh no?” She tried to sidle past her to get to the hallway.

“It puts us in a tricky position – Safia. You could pretend to listen.”

She nodded. “I’m listening. I’m just kind of tired, so – what about – there’s people down there, still, right?”

“They’ll sort them out. What matters is that it further pushes us into an economic corner," her mother said. “And boosts Jupiter even more.”

“Mmhmm,” she said.

“You know Alain Maripuso, don’t you?”

“Sure, I guess. I haven’t spoken to him in ages though.”

“See if he can convince his father to come to stay here. Or in the house on Titan. Say you’ll teach him to ski, or some such.”

“Ok, but Pontmercy hates you, so –”

“So nothing. He benefits just as much as I do from presenting a united front.”

Ah.

But her next race was in under a month, and it would be so very helpful to be down on Titan. “Sure, I’ll get in touch.”

[Callisto, 3800]

“The news this evening: an SPTA team have confirmed that the ‘last man on Saturn’, Callun Connel, has died. Connel, 63, was born on Banach Station in orbit around Jupiter. He was ‘deeply moved’ by news reports from Saturn as a young man, and moved there in 3782, taking the name Zurtir F-1. The SPTA have announced that they will no longer be maintaining the platform on which Connel lived, alongside the few remnants of the mining community.”

[Titan, 3713]

The ridge fell away beneath her. The suit sensed the break and opened wings along her arms and back.

One meter above the ground. Two.

She tilted forward to maintain the arc, thumb hovering over the button for the automated assist. Two-thirds down.

Just beginning to dip below two meters.

She held the angle.

[Callisto, 3726]

“Thirteen years after the Strategic Hydrogen Investment Fund cut shipments to its Saturn hydrogen platforms, the first crewed flights to the atmospheric mining operation since its inception have returned.

“The operation was founded nearly a thousand years ago with a seed population of seven thousand. In late 3713, SHIF records allege their descendants numbered close to half a million.

“Recovery teams have confirmed four hundred and nineteen survivors.

“Yesterday, the unauthorized release of footage taken by the recovery teams has renewed pressure on the Solar Planetary Trade Association to place the Jovian works under direct administration.

“Joining me is Ataraiz M-19, recovered from Saturn with her newborn son, Jatza. Ataraiz, thank you for being here.”

“Hello.”

“And this is your son?”

“Yes.”

“Jatza, is that right?”

“Yes.”

“He is the youngest survivor of the Saturn operation.”

“Yes.”

“You were discharged from hospital only last week. Are you both receiving continuing care?”

“Yes. Jatza still sick. Too thin.”

“There are growing calls now for the SPTA to suspend or revoke SHIF’s remaining hydrogen rights around Jupiter. Have you been following that debate?”

“Don’t know.”

“Of course. Three survivors have reportedly chosen to remain living on one of the mining platforms. What are your thoughts?”

“Is home. I would too, but Jatza.”

“Do you think the Authority has an obligation to maintain the zone for them, despite the cost?”

“Don’t know.”

“Thank you, Ataraiz.”

Passage B:
“Most people have many memories of their mothers. I flatter myself by asserting that I have more. A lifetime of claustrophobically close proximity, as we circled Great Britain. We have lived every moment together – every teenage argument, every moment of grief or joy. I struggle to think of any memory where my mother is not there.

“But when I think of her, I always remember a throwaway comment some twenty years ago. Of course, I am no longer the child of back then, trying to get her attention as she stared at a sunset while we pulled out of Fort William. The sky was always at its best when leaving, she told me. It didn’t make much sense at the time, since we always seemed to be leaving somewhere, but I think the adult that I am now understands a little better.”

Charlotte fumbled for her water glass and took a sip. There was more on the page, the litany of thanks, a string of stupid anecdotes that she found she couldn’t bear the thought of saying. Fuck it all. She set down the cup, spilling a few drops onto the paper.

“May the sky be beautiful for her now, too.”

“Hear, hear!”

She wasn’t sure who said it, but it was enough of an excuse to dip her head and step away. To take the shovel and tip dirt onto her mother’s casket. Her aunt did the same, then that was all the family done and they could all shuffle back towards the fleet of cabs waiting to take them to the station.

They loaded up onto the reception car, which had been set up while they’d been out. She found herself by Maggie, handing out cups of over-milked tea to a crowd which was two thirds fellow passengers and one third random family friends she’d met maybe once in her life. They all knew who she was, of course.

“She was a great woman,” said someone-or-other. “I am so, so sorry for your loss.”

She handed him a cup of tea. “Thank you.”

“So.” Bertie leaned up against the table. “Will the Countess Denham be taking her mother’s seat in the Lords?”

She shoved some tea into his hands. “You just want someone to entertain you.”

“Not an answer, my dear.”

Under them, the train sagged before pulling itself into motion. The passengers barely moved. She reached out to steady the table before the mugs could fall off.

“Imo will have my head if I don’t.” She glanced up, trying to work out where the Baroness of Hexham had gotten to. There – a grey-streaked head bobbing in the midst of a crowd down the far end of the carriage. “It’s something to do, I suppose.”

“What a patriotic way to think about it. Now come. You can’t hide over here all afternoon.”

“I’m hardly hiding!” she protested, but let him pull her into the crowd anyway.

Fucking condolences. A mob of grievers and well-wishers, a parliament in black, pecking at her skin with their half-baked stories about a woman who couldn’t give a damn about any of them, even on the rare occasions that she managed to pull herself out of her own head and notice that there was a world around her. But that was the speech that she chucked out of the window a hundred miles ago – ‘No one was more disappointed by my mother than me. Now she’s dead. God damn it.’ That would have shut them all up.

“Lottie!” Ah, shit. “Oh, dear girl.” Imo grabbed her arm and pulled her into her huddle.

They all looked at her. Half people she’d known all her life, half strangers, all staring at her with their stupid, faux-sad eyes. She did her best to school her face into an appropriate expression of grief.

“Oh, my dear,” said Imo again, patting at her shoulder. “What a hard day it has been for all of us. But you’re bearing up so admirably.”

She nodded, dutifully.

“Have you met my cousins?” she asked.

Charlotte had. Probably. She dug back through a poorly stacked heap of memories of times they’d stopped in Northumberland. “Of course,” she said. “William and Michael Percy. Thank you both for coming. It’d mean a lot to her to know you were here.”

“Of course,” said the one on the left. “She was a great woman.”

She’d hated the Percy family. Hated anyone who’d managed to hold onto their great houses, whose family trusts had emerged any more intact than her own. But let her peers call her a ‘great woman’, let her Wikipedia article declare her the eighth Marquess of Denham and have very little else to say, and let the rest of the world continue on happily without ever concerning itself over her existence.

“I know.”

They stood there for a moment in utter, awkward silence – made infinitely worse by the chatter that bounced up and down the rest of the carriage.

“You know,” said the one on the right, “Michael was actually talking to Imo about joining you all for a few years.”

“Oh?” said Charlotte, grateful for the conversation starter, and to have learned which was Michael and which William.

“It just seems rather an adventure,” said Michael.

“Oh, it’s wonderful.” Imo patted her shoulder. “Wouldn’t you agree, Lottie?”

“Such an adventure,” she agreed.

“I mean, I understand the role of the high speed network but really this does just seem like a much more civilized mode of travel. The two hardly have anything in common.” He glanced upwards out of the window, to where the HS5 track made its way through the sky. “You just can’t see anything from up there. No, if you really want to learn a place, you must travel it slowly. Your eulogy reminded me of that, you know?”

“It did?” asked Charlotte.

“You have to be somewhere to leave it. Properly be somewhere, not zip by.”


[]


“Order!” Imo smacked her hammer against her gavel. There was no notable change in the quiet conversations dotting the room, but she seemed satisfied enough and sat down.

Charlotte leaned over to Bertie. “Is she pretending to be a judge?”

“She believes it lends her noble Ladyship gravitas,” he whispered back.

Charlotte considered that for a second, then shrugged.

“Bet I can set them all off,” he said, grinning like an arse when she glanced at him.

“The floor is now open for questions,” said Imo.

Bertie stood. “My Lords, good afternoon. Once again I find myself obliged to raise the question of the luncheon menu. May I ask whether the noble Lord, the Minister for the Kitchens, might enlighten the House as to when we may expect some new options?”

A chorus of ‘Hear, hear!’ rose up. On the other side of the carriage, Horace McWilliams, Earl of Glencairne, stood. “My Lords, I thank the noble Lord for raising this matter for the sixth sitting in succession. As I informed your Lordships last week, discussions with the kitchen staff are ongoing, and I shall of course report to the House when there is any development.”

“No one likes the lasagna, my Lords!” someone called from the benches.

“My Lords, I am aware that—”

“So change it!”

Another wave of voices rang out as Bertie sat smugly down beside her.

“They’ve been talking about this for five weeks?” she called out, raising her voice over the hubbub.

“Eleven, my Lady!” he shouted back. “I only joined in a month ago.”

The train jolted as it rolled round a corner, and the mace slid from the table in front of Imo. She rose, retrieved it with great dignity, and set it back in its place before sinking down again, her head in her hands.

Eventually she grabbed her hammer again, and smacked it back against the gavel. “Enough!”

The lords took back to their benches, though not without a considerable amount of glaring across the train aisle.

“My Lords, the only business before the House is the Second Reading of the House of Lords Abolition Bill, as brought from the Commons in the year of our Lord 2063, and resubmitted annually thereafter. I call upon the noble Lord, the Earl of Rochester.”

Rochester rose. “My Lords, I fear that once again we gather in dutiful repetition, as we have done each Session for the past forty years, to consider whether we ought to abolish ourselves. Your Lordships will recall that last Session, and the Session before that, and indeed every Session preceding those, we resolved that, however desirable our abolition might appear in principle, the practicalities rendered it most inconvenient.”

The mace fell again. Imo stared at it, and didn’t move. “My Lords, the Question is that the House of Lords Abolition Bill be read a Second time. As many as are of that opinion say ‘Content’.”

Bertie, next to her, said, “Content.” No one else did.

“Of the contrary, ‘Not Content’.”

A much louder chorus chimed up in response. Charlotte said nothing. There did not seem to be much point.

The clerk stood. “Contents, 1. Not-Contents, 97. So the Not-Contents have it.”

“The Bill is, accordingly, rejected. Business being concluded, the House stands adjourned until tomorrow, when we shall resume with the same Bill.”

Everyone stood and shuffled off towards the dining car. “Is that it?” asked Charlotte.

Bertie shrugged. “Imo clearly wasn’t on form today. A shame – usually there’s much more fighting.”
