Passage B:
[Titan, 3713]

She was sweating inside the pressure suit by the time she finished edging her way up the steep hill. Saturn hung overhead, blurred orange by the same atmosphere that had been dragging at her all day. But now she had a moment to catch her breath. She couldn’t see the start of the long descent to Launchpad 23, but the smooth ice of the flat was a far more welcoming prospect than the uneven climb behind her.

She retracted the microspikes along the inside edges of her skis. Nineteen meters per second to fully clear the descent. More than twenty-two and she would risk breaking her leg when the ground flattened out again.

[Interstellar Vessel Flander’s Field, 3822. 27 years of voyage remaining.]

“I was born on Saturn,” the old man tells me. It’s not the first time he’s said it.

He wasn’t old when we boarded, but now he is. Never married, though no one on board ever seemed interested. I’ve never asked why he decided to take the pilgrimage path – perhaps I should have. But I can guess.

“I know,” I say.

“I was the last,” he says, which is also not new. “Everyone dying, and there I was. A baby.” He says it like even he doesn’t believe it. Not really.

“So you’ve said.”

“I was the last,” he repeats.

The doorchime sounds and I open it to let the doctor in. I step out while he does his tests. Take a piss.

He joins me in the corridor after twenty minutes. “You’ll stay with him tonight?” he asks.

“I can,” I say. “Is –”

He shakes his head. “He’s leaving more gently than he came in. You stay with him.”

[L5 Tethys, 3717]

“A word?”

“Maria Callins,” his aide whispered through his earpiece. “Water extraction on Enceladus.”

“M. Callins,” he said.

“Our contract has a buyout clause,” she said, still sitting at the otherwise empty table. No doubt a legacy of burned old earth, back when extraction rights out here were a far lower margin enterprise.

“You’re enforcing it?” he asked.

He’d shown her and the rest of the ‘concerned parties’ the charts. 31.6% of the going rate, under the current contract. All for an operation that had paled beside its sister on Jupiter. In all of their interests, he’d said.

“We’ve upheld our end of the compact. A little consideration would go a long way.” She didn’t smile. She was low-gravity long – shaped by whatever frigid moon gave birth to her.

“We’re freeing you from sales at under a third of what the market would buy your water for,” he said.

“You’re ending a commercial relationship we have taken great pride in maintaining for generations.”

He sat down at the table opposite her, pulling up the chart on the projector again. “Again, this is in all our –”

“And what is your plan for extracting however many bodies you’ve got left down there? We’re all citizens of humanity,” she said, blandly. “I’m a mother, you know?”

There was silence through his earpiece for a second, then, “Maripuso Iceworks. Her daughter married the son last year. Between them, they’re 79% of Saturn-system water production.”

“We’re abiding by our contractual obligations to everyone involved in our proprietary labour solution.”

“You do still have some workers left, don’t you? Because if you’re terminating with us, why, I couldn’t imagine how you’re keeping them hydrated. I know you’re not working with the competi –”

“Fine,” he said.

[Titan, 3713]

Breathing steadied, she shifted her weight forward and pushed into the skate, driving from leg to leg as speed gathered under her. Three meters per second. Five. Eight. Ten. Halfway to the slope now, the ice blurring smooth in the low light. Twelve. Fifteen.

She pushed harder, snapping one ski up before the edge could catch and throw her sideways. Eighteen. Nineteen point three five.

[Interstellar Vessel Flander’s Field, 3801. 48 years of voyage remaining.]

“Don’t stare,” my mother tells me.

“Are you an alien?” I ask, before she can tell me not to.

He’s got two sets of eyelids, the extra one flickering shut as he turns to look into our lit cabin. Doesn’t look human, not even moon-human, long and skinny and always sick. Not like me.

“We’re all aliens,” he says. “Or have you ever been to earth?” He’s smiling when he says it, so he can’t be too upset, but his skin’s shiny like no one I’ve ever seen before.

I shake my head. He’s got an accent that I’ve never heard before, and I used to spend every evening helping my mother out on the docking ports back home. I’ve heard lots of accents.

“I’m from Saturn,” he says. “That’s why I look like this.”

That doesn’t make sense. “I’m from Saturn too,” I say. “We used to live on Enceladus, before –”

“Enough,” my mother says, and pulls me into the cabin, shutting the door.

[Villa Callins, 3713]

Her mother stopped her as she made for bed.

“The shif are closing up shop.”

The words offered up no meaning. Could be some mooner slang from her mother’s youth, could be some corporate acronym she’d just invented. Either way, best to play along. “OK?” she said.

“No more hydrogen extraction. Not here.” Said nice and patronisingly.

“Oh no?” She tried to sidle past her to get to the hallway.

“It puts us in a tricky position – Safia. You could pretend to listen.”

She nodded. “I’m listening. I’m just kind of tired, so – what about – there’s people down there, still, right?”

“They’ll sort them out. What matters is that it further pushes us into an economic corner," her mother said. “And boosts Jupiter even more.”

“Mmhmm,” she said.

“You know Alain Maripuso, don’t you?”

“Sure, I guess. I haven’t spoken to him in ages though.”

“See if he can convince his father to come to stay here. Or in the house on Titan. Say you’ll teach him to ski, or some such.”

“Ok, but Pontmercy hates you, so –”

“So nothing. He benefits just as much as I do from presenting a united front.”

Ah.

But her next race was in under a month, and it would be so very helpful to be down on Titan. “Sure, I’ll get in touch.”

[Callisto, 3800]

“The news this evening: an SPTA team have confirmed that the ‘last man on Saturn’, Callun Connel, has died. Connel, 63, was born on Banach Station in orbit around Jupiter. He was ‘deeply moved’ by news reports from Saturn as a young man, and moved there in 3782, taking the name Zurtir F-1. The SPTA have announced that they will no longer be maintaining the platform on which Connel lived, alongside the few remnants of the mining community.”

[Titan, 3713]

The ridge fell away beneath her. The suit sensed the break and opened wings along her arms and back.

One meter above the ground. Two.

She tilted forward to maintain the arc, thumb hovering over the button for the automated assist. Two-thirds down.

Just beginning to dip below two meters.

She held the angle.

[Callisto, 3726]

“Thirteen years after the Strategic Hydrogen Investment Fund cut shipments to its Saturn hydrogen platforms, the first crewed flights to the atmospheric mining operation since its inception have returned.

“The operation was founded nearly a thousand years ago with a seed population of seven thousand. In late 3713, SHIF records allege their descendants numbered close to half a million.

“Recovery teams have confirmed four hundred and nineteen survivors.

“Yesterday, the unauthorized release of footage taken by the recovery teams has renewed pressure on the Solar Planetary Trade Association to place the Jovian works under direct administration.

“Joining me is Ataraiz M-19, recovered from Saturn with her newborn son, Jatza. Ataraiz, thank you for being here.”

“Hello.”

“And this is your son?”

“Yes.”

“Jatza, is that right?”

“Yes.”

“He is the youngest survivor of the Saturn operation.”

“Yes.”

“You were discharged from hospital only last week. Are you both receiving continuing care?”

“Yes. Jatza still sick. Too thin.”

“There are growing calls now for the SPTA to suspend or revoke SHIF’s remaining hydrogen rights around Jupiter. Have you been following that debate?”

“Don’t know.”

“Of course. Three survivors have reportedly chosen to remain living on one of the mining platforms. What are your thoughts?”

“Is home. I would too, but Jatza.”

“Do you think the Authority has an obligation to maintain the zone for them, despite the cost?”

“Don’t know.”

“Thank you, Ataraiz.”

There was silence through his earpiece for a second, then, “Maripuso Iceworks. Her daughter married the son last year. Between them, they’re 79% of Saturn-system water production.”

“We’re abiding by our contractual obligations to everyone involved in our proprietary labour solution.”

“You do still have some workers left, don’t you? Because if you’re terminating with us, why, I couldn’t imagine how you’re keeping them hydrated. I know you’re not working with the competi –”

“Fine,” he said.

[Titan, 3713]

Breathing steadied, she shifted her weight forward and pushed into the skate, driving from leg to leg as speed gathered under her. Three meters per second. Five. Eight. Ten. Halfway to the slope now, the ice blurring smooth in the low light. Twelve. Fifteen.

She pushed harder, snapping one ski up before the edge could catch and throw her sideways. Eighteen. Nineteen point three five.

[Interstellar Vessel Flander’s Field, 3801. 48 years of voyage remaining.]

“Don’t stare,” my mother tells me.

“Are you an alien?” I ask, before she can tell me not to.

He’s got two sets of eyelids, the extra one flickering shut as he turns to look into our lit cabin. Doesn’t look human, not even moon-human, long and skinny and always sick. Not like me.

“We’re all aliens,” he says. “Or have you ever been to earth?” He’s smiling when he says it, so he can’t be too upset, but his skin’s shiny like no one I’ve ever seen before.

I shake my head. He’s got an accent that I’ve never heard before, and I used to spend every evening helping my mother out on the docking ports back home. I’ve heard lots of accents.

“I’m from Saturn,” he says. “That’s why I look like this.”

That doesn’t make sense. “I’m from Saturn too,” I say. “We used to live on Enceladus, before –”

“Enough,” my mother says, and pulls me into the cabin, shutting the door.

[Villa Callins, 3713]

Her mother stopped her as she made for bed.

“The shif are closing up shop.”

The words offered up no meaning. Could be some mooner slang from her mother’s youth, could be some corporate acronym she’d just invented. Either way, best to play along. “OK?” she said.

“No more hydrogen extraction. Not here.” Said nice and patronisingly.

“Oh no?” She tried to sidle past her to get to the hallway.

“It puts us in a tricky position – Safia. You could pretend to listen.”

She nodded. “I’m listening. I’m just kind of tired, so – what about – there’s people down there, still, right?”

“They’ll sort them out. What matters is that it further pushes us into an economic corner," her mother said. “And boosts Jupiter even more.”

“Mmhmm,” she said.

“You know Alain Maripuso, don’t you?”

“Sure, I guess. I haven’t spoken to him in ages though.”

“See if he can convince his father to come to stay here. Or in the house on Titan. Say you’ll teach him to ski, or some such.”

“Ok, but Pontmercy hates you, so –”

“So nothing. He benefits just as much as I do from presenting a united front.”

Ah.

But her next race was in under a month, and it would be so very helpful to be down on Titan. “Sure, I’ll get in touch.”

[Callisto, 3800]

“The news this evening: an SPTA team have confirmed that the ‘last man on Saturn’, Callun Connel, has died. Connel, 63, was born on Banach Station in orbit around Jupiter. He was ‘deeply moved’ by news reports from Saturn as a young man, and moved there in 3782, taking the name Zurtir F-1. The SPTA have announced that they will no longer be maintaining the platform on which Connel lived, alongside the few remnants of the mining community.”

[Titan, 3713]

The ridge fell away beneath her. The suit sensed the break and opened wings along her arms and back.

One meter above the ground. Two.

She tilted forward to maintain the arc, thumb hovering over the button for the automated assist. Two-thirds down.

Just beginning to dip below two meters.

She held the angle.

[Callisto, 3726]

“Thirteen years after the Strategic Hydrogen Investment Fund cut shipments to its Saturn hydrogen platforms, the first crewed flights to the atmospheric mining operation since its inception have returned.

“The operation was founded nearly a thousand years ago with a seed population of seven thousand. In late 3713, SHIF records allege their descendants numbered close to half a million.

“Recovery teams have confirmed four hundred and nineteen survivors.

“Yesterday, the unauthorized release of footage taken by the recovery teams has renewed pressure on the Solar Planetary Trade Association to place the Jovian works under direct administration.

“Joining me is Ataraiz M-19, recovered from Saturn with her newborn son, Jatza. Ataraiz, thank you for being here.”

“Hello.”

“And this is your son?”

“Yes.”

“Jatza, is that right?”

“Yes.”

“He is the youngest survivor of the Saturn operation.”

“Yes.”

“You were discharged from hospital only last week. Are you both receiving continuing care?”

“Yes. Jatza still sick. Too thin.”

“There are growing calls now for the SPTA to suspend or revoke SHIF’s remaining hydrogen rights around Jupiter. Have you been following that debate?”

“Don’t know.”

“Of course. Three survivors have reportedly chosen to remain living on one of the mining platforms. What are your thoughts?”

“Is home. I would too, but Jatza.”

“Do you think the Authority has an obligation to maintain the zone for them, despite the cost?”

“Don’t know.”

“Thank you, Ataraiz.”

Passage B:
I’m a good person, I promise. I didn’t say that to the Brownies as I crossed their picket line, but I did feel bad about it. Not so bad as to want to spend any more time letting them sling mud my way than I had to. But bad nonetheless. The Wizard Andrew Macallister was not someone, I suspect, well versed in opening his own door. He stood awkwardly, blocking the entryway, staring at me for a very long moment while the six Brownies and four Ghillie Dhus outside kicked their protest up another notch.

I smiled at him. “Hi. Dana Ross.” Stuck out my hand for him to look dumbfounded at.

“Ah,” he said at last. “The help.”

“That’s me!” I kept it light and cheerful as a glob of mud smacked into the back of my head. He still didn’t move as it made its wet way down my neck. I’d worn the nice white shirt that Chris bought me for job interviews, back in The Day, and I could feel the collar sogging against my skin.

Finally he worked out how to step aside. I wasted no time getting inside the white walls of his entrance hall, and he wasted none getting the door shut behind me. The mud fell and hit the floorboards.

Andrew Macallister had the professorial look down. Slightly overlarge black suit, chalk dust on the cuffs, and an unnaturally full head of grey hair.

I took pity on him. “Why don’t you show me where you keep your cleaning stuff? I’ll get that sorted before your guests arrive.”

“Supplies?” he asked.

Brownies. Right.

“Where’s the loo?” I tried.

He pointed me to the toilet, where I took a moment to wash my shirt. They’d managed to get mud into my hair as well; I wound up with almost my whole head in the sink, before all the brown was washed out of my dull orange curls. There was some sort of noise cancelling spelled into the walls of the house. None of the shouts made their way in. Even the entryway was perfectly calm as I took some loo paper to wipe up the mess my entrance and the Brownies' good aim had made.

It was the kitchen of a wizard who wanted you to know it. Why have a fridge when you can pull the edge of an arctic gale through exposed shelving? The only thing out of place was me in my nylon tights. That was the problem with ancestral traditions, I supposed. Sometimes they decide they want their milk organic. Or whatever Macallister’d managed to do to upset them.

I grabbed the boxes of M&S canapes, and started laying them out on the antique-looking trays he had set up on his counter. The wizard himself was through the double doors, arms full of bottles of champagne that he plonked on the table in his much-too-large-even-for-Clifton garden. He had a whole bloody forest back there. That explained the Ghillie Dhus, I supposed.

It might have been a few years since my teenage stint at a catering company, but I fancy I did a decent enough job as a one-man band once his gaggle of fellow academics materialized. They got to enter through the back gate, where I greeted them with champagne and cocktail sausages. And once they were all tipsily gathered around a glyph-filled textbook, arguing over the most efficient way to do some exercise on levitation theory, I turned to the washing up.

A few of the guests drifted inside once or twice seeking refills, or the loo, or both. The fourth of them stopped briefly behind me. I kept washing up as something ice cold slipped into my trouser pocket. And then she was gone, and all that remained was the chill biting into my thigh. It was impossible to get a sense of shape from just the way it pressed – at least a little bit pointy – but no.

There was nothing in my pocket.

I kept washing up.

About ten minutes later, they moved the party inside.

“Oh, let me dry.” One of the PhD students, the one whose textbook it was, grabbed a dishcloth.

“Thanks,” I said and smiled at him.

“Where do the glasses go?” asked another, reaching for the one in his hand. “Gimme that, Pranav.”

Pranav. Well, that saved me seeking him out.

The grownup academics seemed content to let them pay their servile dues, keeping their argument going around the kitchen table instead.

“Did you work out the answer?” I asked Pranav.

“Yeah, but they’re stuck on whether it’s more efficient to magnetize your object, or mess with its gravity.”

“Magnetic enough to spontaneously levitate?” I asked, casting an eye at the gathered arcanists, who had started drawing on one of the boxes for the champagne glasses. The silverware had looked like actual silver when I saw it earlier, but that could just as easily be bespelled stainless steel.

He grinned at me, toothy and lopsided. “It won’t work. I tried it a few days ago. Prof Macallister just doesn’t want to admit I’m right.”

“Right about?” I smiled back.

“You just put it on the memory of an object. Boom, problem solved. But then Professor Tangible would have to let me write my thesis on the permanent, so –”

“Uh huh,” I said. My leg was getting numb where the pointy bit was digging in.

“Pranav!” called Professor Tangible. Good. He’d kept an eye on his student.

He turned away to look at his teacher, who was setting the now scribble-covered box atop a spell circle embedded in his countertop.

“This is why we work with what nature prov – ah.”

The cutlery drawer, to my right, burst open and about half the forks and six-odd butter knives went flying out. The cardboard box did indeed levitate for the briefest of moments as they stabbed into it. Then the whole sorry ensemble crashed to the floor, bringing two of the glasses with it.

“Alright,” I said. “Everyone stay still. Where’s your dustpan and – right.”

I left them pretending to be statues, while I went back into the hall in search of something to use other than my bare hands. While he did have an understairs cupboard, the Brownies had turned it into a bit of a hangout spot. I couldn’t imagine the polyester beanbag was Macallister’s, but the quilt atop it was made of J-cloths and yellow dusters, and they’d jury-rigged something together from the guts of a vacuum cleaner. Henry’s smiling face had been cracked in two to reveal the motor that served as his metal heart. The hose burrowed its way out below the floorboards; presumably a way to get some air into this airless cupboard. But in his current state, he was entirely useless to me.

I regretted it. Even as I did it, I regretted it. It was for a good cause. In my own way, I would be helping them. In the end. But I took that quilt into the kitchen where Macallister was scribbling over the symbols he’d written on the box, and I used the scissors that were now no longer stuck to it to unpick the thread around one of the dusters and I used it to pick up the glass, to wipe up the champagne, before wrapping the whole mess in the rest of the quilt, and threw it all in the bin.

The party was over. That much was clear. Macallister shooed off the students into the garden where they vanished through whatever gate they’d entered in by.

intro: I'd like your view on two passages.
prompt:
I'd like your view on two passages.

For this comparison, please read both passages carefully before making your choice.

Passage A:
Dunnest Smoke

Among the things we are busy not talking about: the chicken in the fridge has gone off and is starting to smell; the dog’s limp has gotten worse but no one wants to make the call on amputating versus putting her down; and on the forecast this morning it said that the clouds came down three metres today, an increase on the steady two-point-eight of the last week.

Mum and I went up the hill today, first time she’s been out in days – add to the list: Mum has not been getting out enough and is starting to develop bedsores – and the top was covered. Few weeks ago, you could see over the Bristol Channel to Wales. But there were photos of the top of the clouds from skyscrapers on the BBC this morning, sunlit gold and pink. Hope, apparently, sunny blue skies if we can only hold on.

Most days, my dad sits in the kitchen with his tablet, filling the room with some arse or other going on about trans people. He calls me over. “Frankie, have a look at this.”

“You shouldn’t watch that stuff,” I tell him every time. Try to show as little reaction as possible.

“Always so serious,” he says. Then he turns it off. He’s got what he wanted, now he’ll get back to the crossword.

In the background, Grandpa sits in the corner. Can never tell if his hearing aid’s in or not, but that’s how he likes it. After all, another thing we never mention: he and Dad can’t stand each other. Grandpa used to play footie — now he’s an eighty-four-year-old conspiracy nut who wants to open all our eyes to the truth. Meanwhile Dad’s one YouTube Short from a full-on three-quarter-life crisis and doesn’t much like the vision he’s getting of his future. Deals with it by making it obvious he thinks Grandpa’s an old bigot (we also don’t talk about the pot meet kettle of it all).

“Frankie,” says Grandpa, “do you have a minute?”

Of course. “Of course.”

“Did you get my email?” he asks. Taps his tablet. “I sent you an article.”

The answer is yes, but I gave up at the headline: ‘Who Controls the Weather? How Governments Are Playing God With the Atmosphere.’

“Is it a pressing matter?” whispers Dad.

I give him a sideways glance. “I wouldn’t say that wisdom descended from above.”

Grandpa shakes his head. “You’ll have to repeat that, Frankie.”

“Oh, sorry.” I say. “It wasn’t anything interesting.”

He sits there for a moment. “Well, you ought to read the article.”

I glance behind me. Dad’s smirking, obviously. Best foot forward: I nod. Not enough. “I will?” That does it.

“That-a girl,” he tells me, and lets me go.

I can hear Mum making her way up the stairs, breathing heavily. The walk didn’t do her as much good as I’d hoped, but we try not to mention the fact that they never do. It’ll be a few days minimum before we can get her out again, now that it’s never sunny. Seasonal affective disorder gone mad.

Another truth unspoken: the electric bill’s gone haywire in the last few months. Mum’s always got the lights and the heating on upstairs, and we’ve got them on in the kitchen. Can’t complain about it, because it depresses her. Don’t want to sit in the dark.

Damned Spot looks up from her bed, struggles upright and limps to me, looking for a cuddle. I give her one. Used to be, even a week ago, she’d have followed Mum up to bed and lain at her feet for her nap. Didn’t even try to come on our walk today. I get my fingers right where she likes them, behind her ears, set her tail to its long, easy wags.

“Good girl,” I tell her firmly. By the door, her food bowl is picked at and she’s unreceptive to my attempts to get her to eat.

“Probably needs the loo,” my dad says.

I head for the door. “Out, Damned Spot?” I say, because that’s what we always say, and maybe her ears perk up. Or I’m just seeing what I want to. Either way, we stumble our five-legged way outside, where we stand on the grass under the low, thick grey of the sky for one minute, two, five.

Damned Spot stares around, brown-eyed and unquestioning, and doesn’t do her business or anything else. Eventually, tips of my fingers beginning to get cold, we stumble our five-legged way back in.

“Ought to be shot,” says Grandpa. “Kindest thing for it.”

Dad whistles her over and she goes to him, slow and struggling. “She’s got a bit of life in her yet,” he says, leans over to give her a proper stroke and nearly unbalances her. “Don’t you, girl?”

I go over to the fridge, open it, then shut it again before the smell of the chicken can escape.

“Snack supper?” I say and Dad laughs.

Mum’s been on the Austen miniseries again, decides we’re watching the new Persuasion ‘as a family’. Grandpa sits in the armchair with his whiskey and sips silently, eyes fixed on the far wall. Heating hasn’t been on in the sitting room for weeks and the damp’s got into the sofa so I’m buried under a blanket.

“Put it away,” Mum hisses. It’s more alive than I’ve heard her in a minute. Scares me out of my skin, and I do my best to look like I’m paying attention.

But I’m not the one in trouble. Dad sighs and puts his phone on the arm of the sofa next to him. Grandpa, in his chair, hums and sips.

It’s not a very good film.

Ten or so minutes pass before Mum stands up.

“I’m going to bed,” she tells us, and then she’s gone.

Dad’s straight back on his phone. He pokes at it for a while until there’s no more footsteps above us.

“I’ll go check on the mutt,” he says. Then he, too, leaves.

I can hear his voice quietly in the kitchen, then the back door opens. A few minutes later it closes and quiet footsteps make their way upstairs. They’ll be in different rooms tonight, or she’ll kick up a fuss about him not finishing watching.

I sit and scroll until the credits roll, then turn off the TV. Grandpa’s asleep. His glass is empty on the side table next to him, and his glasses are half-way falling off his face.

I should wake him up, probably. Get him to go to bed.

I fold up the blanket and hang it over the sofa and turn off the lights before heading off to my room. Check my emails before I go to sleep. Delete the promotions and the subscriptions and the article, then turn off my phone and do my best to keep warm.

Maybe I’m still hungry, maybe I feel bad about leaving Grandpa down there, or maybe I just can’t sleep, but at four in the morning I wake up and go downstairs. I check in the sitting room, but he’s not in there, though his glass is. I pick it up and wander into the kitchen in search of a bowl of cereal. As soon as I turn the light on, I see her.

Damned Spot lies on the floor of the kitchen, wheezing harsh breaths in and out. A part of me knows that I should call my parents, that I should call the vet, but in the moment I just go to her and I sink to my knees and bury my hands in her fur.

“Good girl,” I tell her, as scared brown eyes meet mine. “Good dog. It’s alright.”

I stay there, stay slowly stroking her, as she goes still, spasms, goes still again.

“I want to bury her on the hill,” Mum insists, and so up we go while Dad carries Damned Spot, until we hit the cloud, just a bit lower than it was yesterday. Grandpa follows and his eyes watch everything.

“You know, we never buried our dogs,” he tells us, and I want to hit him or scream but I don’t do anything because we certainly never talk about the ways he’s awful in front of him or Mum.

Sam from the village is waiting up top with a digger by a freshly dug hole, only visible when we get close; he looms through cloud thick enough to make everything up here feel close and damp.

“Alright?” he says, sounding uncomfortable.

Dad thanks him, and Sam from the village nods before slowly driving back to the works over the road.

“I can’t bear it,” Mum informs us all, and staggers off by herself into the cloud.

That leaves Dad and me to lower her into the hole and push all the dirt on top, lay flat the grass turf, and shove in a stick to mark it.

“We should’ve brought a stone.”

“Should’ve had her cremated, really,” says Dad. “Much more efficient use of space. You know, they mix up all the ashes, scoop a bunch out and stick ‘em in a jar. ‘S not much point crying over a bunch of bits of other people’s pets.”

Grandpa’s standing off there in the mist, looking around as though thinking of all the places he’d rather be. “We never bothered with any of this, you know. Just told the vet to take it with them when he was done.”

Dad nudges me. “Maybe we should tell the doctor to do the same with him, hey?”

I don’t cry. I just stand there, as Grandpa goes wandering off. I’m glad for it, really. Glad he’s not saying anything else. I don’t think I could bear it.

There’s a moment where Dad and I stand around in the cloud, him silent and awkward and still waiting for me to cry or laugh, before he sighs and jerks his head. I step away and follow him, as we begin making our way after Mum.

She’s gone to the very top of the hill, where there’s a small trig point, just a bit of rock left to mark out the highest point, and is staring out into the endless, endlessly close fog.

“You know,” she says, and she sounds terribly far away. “I think I can see Wales.”

Dad takes her arm, guides her to lean on him, and the two begin to oh-so-slowly walk down the hill.

Grandpa touches my shoulder, and he won’t say it, but it is an apology. I keep my peace, and we follow them down.

They’re already in by the time we get there, boots on the rack, but nowhere to be seen.

“I’ll have a shower, I think,” Grandpa tells me and I’m ready for him to go upstairs but instead he follows me into the kitchen.

I watch him grab the washing-up liquid.

“Shower gel,” he says. Laughs, winks, and then he’s off with it in hand.

I stand there for a second. “What?”

But there’s only me in here now.

I never got that midnight snack, so I wander over to the fridge. Open it. The smell, unleashed, fills the room and I should shut the door and open the windows and put away Spot’s water bowl because she’ll not be needing it anymore and

I take the pack of chicken drumsticks out the fridge, slimy and discoloured and half-covered by a flapping lip of clear plastic that does nothing to stop the assault of their reek. And I put it on the counter and I leave it there to fill the whole room with its rot.

Here are the things that I’m going to do. I’m going to kick on the flip-flops by the door and I’m going to flip and flop my way outside and I will flip and flop my way all the way back up that hill. And I will lose a shoe three or four times; that’s inevitable. When I get there, I won’t be able to see Wales, but I will tell myself that up above me, amidst all the clouds, there’s a patch that’s a lighter shade of grey.

(By the time I come down, the chicken’s in the bin, uncovered, and the door to the kitchen’s shut. I can hear some nasally American accent coming from the sitting room, occasionally stuttering because the WiFi’s not so good in there. But that’s fine. I grab the bin bag and shove it — still open — into the hall.)

Passage B:
We walk. All along the lowway, me in front and Little Fellow in the middle and Him somewhere in back. Slow progress, little steps for little legs, but still walking on. In the water, waist lanterns dancing white as we march. Everywhere, up on the drainways, ducking under the pipes, on the bridges crossing here down below. And once, tonight, another walker with their light-bright legs. Flash our lantern signs through the night - hello, goodbye, beware below, beware to walk. We cross when we see that one: up the ladders that moss and mist make sticky, to the first drainway, over the connector, then back to the lowways and the walking on.

Up in the city, yellow-gold up-above where the lights don’t dance, they turn yellow-dim then gone. The sky greys, and where the air can reach, skin pricks wet and suffers for it. Low water, say the city-lights in their fading. Low water and clear skies. But the water’s always low if you’re up there.

He pushes past Little Fellow and grabs at me when I turn around so I don’t have to hear him. “Stop,” he says, hands loud and clear. No nonsense hands. I-know-best hands. “Morning. Red sky. We go up.”

I shut my eyes. Feel Little Fellow put his hand in mine and turn, blind, walk on.

Only open them when I’m sure He’s behind me where I don’t have to listen. Keep going, past one tent up on the drainway on the other side. Little Fellow walks slow now. I’ve got his hand, pull him with me. Keep going till the thin little sky gets bloody on its chin.

That’s when his hand gets pulled out of mine. He’s got Little Fellow over his shoulder, is climbing up-and-up one hand then step-step then one hand then step-step.

“Stop!” I yell, arms jerking with it, but he’s the one not looking now. No point.

I get on the ladder, up after him. Up all the lowways, onto the drainways, but it's getting thick-air hot, skin beginning to prick and sting, goggles fogging and mask clogging and he pulls off the ladder well before we’re up past the floodline. Mumbles something, like he’s mouthspeaking behind his mask.

He leads a bit further, carrying Little Fellow, so I have to follow. It’s burning properly now. Not quite rash-deep but not so far off – worse for Little Fellow. He gets us to where Up’s been doing work on one of the drains.

“Climb,” he says. Order.

I climb up their scaffold to the platform just below the round of the great pipe where it sticks out from the squished bones of the old city. It’s hard – I’m a good climber, lifetime of climbing, keeping light. But it’s hard. Hot hard, sweat hard – new metal, not yet rust-rough to give something to stick to. Smooth, not slick. It’s not meant to be climbed, either. They come down to it, after all. But I get up there, because I have to. Reach down to take Little Fellow from him and pull him up next to me. He gets up after us, gets his tent out of his pack and pulls the trigger to pop it up. It’s a small tent, one-man tent, not nice and big like the one I left with ma. But Little Fellow and I can curl up on one side and He sticks on the other and doesn’t try to touch me. Still have ma’s knife, after all.

We get into the tent. Get the pump going. Sit as far away from him as we can get – not very far. I’ve got the cooker, ma’s cooker – trying not to worry about it – and the food, though we’re running low – trying not to worry about it, she’ll bring more when she finds us. Get two packs boiling while he gets his roll laid out. Split it three ways. Wish I didn’t, but it’s his tent. Them’s the rules, says ma, from wherever she is.

I get Little Fellow his comic from my pack. Let him sit and lean on the wall while I get our sleep-clothes out and bedding set up, get changed. He goes to sit next to him.

“What does that say?” he asks.

Little Fellow turns the page. Doesn’t like mouth-speaking, but He does it anyway.

“Come on, Darra,” he says. “How about that. T-H-R-O-U-G-H. What’s that spell?”

“Not his name,” I mouth-say.

He ignores me, but Little Fellow also ignores him, so we both know who’s right. I know what he’s thinking about: sneak away in the day, take Little Fellow. Leave me to chase after, just like ma. But I learned from her. I know to hold on tight enough that I’ll wake up if he tries.

Get him stripped and changed into sleep-soft fabric. Hang up our sweat-wet inners to dry over the day. The air’s blistered him a bit around his cheeks.

“Soothe,” I say, and reach behind me for him to give it over. Rub it into the sores even as he squirms and wiggles about.

“We have to stop earlier,” he says. “Aika –”

“Not my name.”

He sighs. “You’re hurting the lad.”

“Not your problem.”

“Yes it is.” He reaches past to take Little Fellow’s empty bowl, scrapes the rest of his food into it, and hands it back to him. “He’s my son, Aika – Eyecut. It falls to me to step in where you and your mother have fallen short.”

I rinse our dishes and pack them up, get us both curled up and facing away from him. Hear him get changed somewhere behind us. He won’t be looking so I can turn my head around and peek. Makes sense to me, why he had to pay ma for it. Back when I was as small as Little Fellow. He’s weird under the mask. Big blobby nose and pale eyes and no lips, burn-spotted skin. I wouldn’t fuck him even if he paid me. Maybe he wasn’t as ugly then.

The flood comes while we sleep. Up and up, while the rain pushes down and down, soaking sodden wood to saturation until all the world is grey and brown.

I’m half awake, have to be, have to hold on to Little Fellow. Doesn’t take much to make me all the way awake. Scramble over to ma, have to – except its not ma, but it doesn’t matter, not right now.

“Wha –” and then the rain turns his stupid face grey and brown. “Get everything packed! Now, Aika.”

Doesn’t have to tell me, because I’m already folding the cooker, getting our walkwear into the pack. No time for anything more than getting my arm through the straps of our masks, wrapping Little Fellow up in his outer. Can’t stop to change. Get out into the wet. Wet, wet everywhere – no need to guess what they were doing to the pipe, because water’s pouring out from around it, some crack buried deep in the old-brick mire. Not on top of us, but the metal’s death-smooth where we’ll have to climb down. The tent pops down and I grab it, grab Little Fellow – stupid, stupid, I know it’s stupid – start trying to climb, no arms, just legs. Passage B:
Gilbert is Dead

Murder, squawk the geese, the rooster, the rooks in parliament, who saw it all go down (and then, presumably, back up again). Murder most fowl. And I, innocence proven by the fact that I do not have a car, stop halfway down the drive. I kneel by the corpse. I will play detective and mourner and mortuary, since Gilbert is dead.

It does not hurt that he is down a leg, bottom half gnawed away. Herself’s camera whirls to follow me as I bring the coffin through the morning-empty yard.

It is not a particularly involved task, the pressing of a button. But it is hers; she takes to it with all the pomp and bureaucracy of the civil servant she no longer is.

“Oh,” she says. “Did you get your A-levels? Results today, aren’t they?”

“Gilbert is dead,” I tell them. There is no point softening it.

Herself wheezes in as though she has been twice run over herself, and then eaten by a fox. Himself sets down his iPad.

“Is he in there?” he asks.

I nod, and show him the contents of the box.

“Who could have done this?” she asks. Beside her, the kettle begins to boil before turning itself off. “I spoke to Hansen about getting a Mabel replacement only this morning!”

“A fox,” I say.

“Certainly not,” Herself concurs. “Perhaps the cat?”

The cat, halfway out the metaphorical door, rarely steps through the material one. And besides, “He was a turkey,” I remind Themselves. “Big. I can look into it if you want, but –”

“Oh, what a good idea,” Himself says.

“Yes – if someone is killing our animals, we must get to the bottom of it. Our duty of care.”

I stand there for a little longer, holding the box. “Would you like me to leave him here?”

“No –” “-- yes” “Well –”

I set the box down by the door, and back away. Their King Charles spaniel looks as though he’s about to have a sniff, but I push him back inside and make my way to the yard.

“Gilbert is dead,” I tell Tommo, who’s just arrived. “Hit by a car.”

“Wasn’t me,” he says, immediately.

“I won’t tell if it was.”

I truly won’t. Tommo has committed no unforgivable sin, save for the unfortunate fact that he’s rather attractive. And also that he could have gone to uni, his mother being both educated and somewhat wealthy, and chose for whatever reason to spend his life running a mad woman’s hobby farm.

“Still wasn’t me. Maybe it was Mabel’s ghost?” He grins. “Scorned her in life, eh, now she’s back?”

“It was a car and a fox.”

That gets him to stop fiddling about in the back of his van.

“Another bloody fox? What’d you do with the rest of him?”

“Don’t know what else would’ve eaten him. And he’s by the kitchen. Why?”

“String him up to bait that fox tonight, that’s for why.”

I grimace. “Himself won’t like that.”

Tommo shrugs. And then he sets himself to rummaging. He’s an excellent rummager, spends most of every day at it, vehicle large enough that he might rummage at his leisure with all the appearance of diligence.

But the thing with vans – or at least with this van, I claim no broader expertise – is that it has wide tyres. Wider than the tread of whatever hit Gilbert twice over, which did not strike me (or him), as being of unusual dimension. While his back is turned, I angle myself to get a better view of how much of their surface is in contact with the ground. Too much.

“What was their friend called, the one who was about over the weekend?”

“How should I know?” says Tommo.

I usually don’t work on the weekends. But this Saturday, I was called in by none other than Herself to go for a ‘spin’ in their friend’s convertible Audi. Now, why someone would have a convertible in the wet South West is beyond me, nor can I explain what made her decide that it would be an experience so life-changing that I had to give up my afternoon, but the summons was sent and, faithfully, I obeyed.

The ride was unremarkable; I will remark no more upon it. The car itself, however. It was no doubt expensive, but I cannot think of a number that could hope to capture the value it seemed to hold for our poor, dead Gilbert.

I cannot claim him to have been deprived, even after Mabel left him – and the rest of us – for a fox’s tender embrace. She had never been of much interest to him, not while there were slippers, towels, and roosters in the world. And those things persisted, even when she did not. But the Audi – my god, the Audi. You see, mornings (as far as any of us could tell) on the farm usually featured Gilbert in the kitchen, perched atop Himself’s slipper. Himself would be playing chess on his iPad and Gilbert would be… rustling. An odd way of going about things, but we must allow for oddities in this life. Bad for the planned industrial sale of Christmas turkeys, slippers being reproductively incompatible with poultry, but that was Herself’s to concern Herself with.

And then, we must presume, Gilbert saw the Audi. With its canvas top and shiny paint, not even a little mud splattered. And Gilbert loved the Audi. Passionately. Furiously. Extensively and expensively. I bore witness to it on Saturday. We got out of the car and he got on it, and he went for a ride rather more satisfying than our own.

Birds will be birds, Himself said (as I recall) and laughed.

Hm, Herself said, and she certainly did not sound happy.

“Do you have access to the camera?” I ask Tommo. I don’t, because I am not Our Lady’s beloved surrogate son.

“Sure,” he says, and fiddles about on his phone before handing it to me and going back to rummaging.

I watch through Saturday evening, watch Gilbert settle himself to sleep atop his beloved. Sunday – the car remains beturkeyed through much of the day, with a brief appearance from two of the geese in a failed territory grab. Given that their friend is clearly gone this morning, and there is no car here, I had assumed that he’d driven off in it, but instead a taxi arrives and he leaves therein. Gilbert gives a brief, futile chase up the drive and out of sight before reappearing. He sits himself back atop his love and settles himself down to roost.

Nothing triggers the camera until this morning. Not Himself wandering into the yard to fetch wood, not the dog emptying itself, nothing. Certainly no car leaving.

The next thing it catches is me coming down, Gilbert in box. And there is no Audi in the yard.

I head back to the kitchen.

The box is gone, as is Himself. Herself is still standing by the kettle, her head bowed as she waits for it to boil.

“A fox killed him,” I say. “Tommo says he’ll set bait up tonight.”

“Oh,” is all she says.

“When will the new turkeys be arriving?” I ask. I’m still holding Tommo’s phone and she looks at it as she turns around.

“Hansen says he has some chicks in. I’ll pick them up tomorrow, if you could set up the stable.”

“Of course.”

“You’ll tell the others, won’t you?”

“If they ask, I’ll tell them a fox did it. That’s the truth, isn’t it?”

There is steam coming up from the kettle behind her. Once again, it turns itself off.

“We’re having to pay to repaint David’s car,” she says. “He wouldn’t come back if the turkey was – if – and that damn bird was always in here. With my husband.”

I don’t say anything.

“Anyway, like you said. A fox did it.”

“Quite so,” I say. “Oh, I was going to tell you, but I got distracted by the whole Gilbert thing. I made my grades for UCL. Economics.”

“Well done!” she says.

“I’m not sure if I’ll take it.” I wander in, shutting the door behind me. “I’d like to. But the cost of living, well –”

“I see,” she says.

Passage B:
Dunnest Smoke

Among the things we are busy not talking about: the chicken in the fridge has gone off and is starting to smell; the dog’s limp has gotten worse but no one wants to make the call on amputating versus putting her down; and on the forecast this morning it said that the clouds came down three metres today, an increase on the steady two-point-eight of the last week.

Mum and I went up the hill today, first time she’s been out in days – add to the list: Mum has not been getting out enough and is starting to develop bedsores – and the top was covered. Few weeks ago, you could see over the Bristol Channel to Wales. But there were photos of the top of the clouds from skyscrapers on the BBC this morning, sunlit gold and pink. Hope, apparently, sunny blue skies if we can only hold on.

Most days, my dad sits in the kitchen with his tablet, filling the room with some arse or other going on about trans people. He calls me over. “Frankie, have a look at this.”

“You shouldn’t watch that stuff,” I tell him every time. Try to show as little reaction as possible.

“Always so serious,” he says. Then he turns it off. He’s got what he wanted, now he’ll get back to the crossword.

In the background, Grandpa sits in the corner. Can never tell if his hearing aid’s in or not, but that’s how he likes it. After all, another thing we never mention: he and Dad can’t stand each other. Grandpa used to play footie — now he’s an eighty-four-year-old conspiracy nut who wants to open all our eyes to the truth. Meanwhile Dad’s one YouTube Short from a full-on three-quarter-life crisis and doesn’t much like the vision he’s getting of his future. Deals with it by making it obvious he thinks Grandpa’s an old bigot (we also don’t talk about the pot meet kettle of it all).

“Frankie,” says Grandpa, “do you have a minute?”

Of course. “Of course.”

“Did you get my email?” he asks. Taps his tablet. “I sent you an article.”

The answer is yes, but I gave up at the headline: ‘Who Controls the Weather? How Governments Are Playing God With the Atmosphere.’

“Is it a pressing matter?” whispers Dad.

I give him a sideways glance. “I wouldn’t say that wisdom descended from above.”

Grandpa shakes his head. “You’ll have to repeat that, Frankie.”

“Oh, sorry.” I say. “It wasn’t anything interesting.”

He sits there for a moment. “Well, you ought to read the article.”

I glance behind me. Dad’s smirking, obviously. Best foot forward: I nod. Not enough. “I will?” That does it.

“That-a girl,” he tells me, and lets me go.

I can hear Mum making her way up the stairs, breathing heavily. The walk didn’t do her as much good as I’d hoped, but we try not to mention the fact that they never do. It’ll be a few days minimum before we can get her out again, now that it’s never sunny. Seasonal affective disorder gone mad.

Another truth unspoken: the electric bill’s gone haywire in the last few months. Mum’s always got the lights and the heating on upstairs, and we’ve got them on in the kitchen. Can’t complain about it, because it depresses her. Don’t want to sit in the dark.

Damned Spot looks up from her bed, struggles upright and limps to me, looking for a cuddle. I give her one. Used to be, even a week ago, she’d have followed Mum up to bed and lain at her feet for her nap. Didn’t even try to come on our walk today. I get my fingers right where she likes them, behind her ears, set her tail to its long, easy wags.

“Good girl,” I tell her firmly. By the door, her food bowl is picked at and she’s unreceptive to my attempts to get her to eat.

“Probably needs the loo,” my dad says.

I head for the door. “Out, Damned Spot?” I say, because that’s what we always say, and maybe her ears perk up. Or I’m just seeing what I want to. Either way, we stumble our five-legged way outside, where we stand on the grass under the low, thick grey of the sky for one minute, two, five.

Damned Spot stares around, brown-eyed and unquestioning, and doesn’t do her business or anything else. Eventually, tips of my fingers beginning to get cold, we stumble our five-legged way back in.

“Ought to be shot,” says Grandpa. “Kindest thing for it.”

Dad whistles her over and she goes to him, slow and struggling. “She’s got a bit of life in her yet,” he says, leans over to give her a proper stroke and nearly unbalances her. “Don’t you, girl?”

I go over to the fridge, open it, then shut it again before the smell of the chicken can escape.

“Snack supper?” I say and Dad laughs.

Mum’s been on the Austen miniseries again, decides we’re watching the new Persuasion ‘as a family’. Grandpa sits in the armchair with his whiskey and sips silently, eyes fixed on the far wall. Heating hasn’t been on in the sitting room for weeks and the damp’s got into the sofa so I’m buried under a blanket.

“Put it away,” Mum hisses. It’s more alive than I’ve heard her in a minute. Scares me out of my skin, and I do my best to look like I’m paying attention.

But I’m not the one in trouble. Dad sighs and puts his phone on the arm of the sofa next to him. Grandpa, in his chair, hums and sips.

It’s not a very good film.

Ten or so minutes pass before Mum stands up.

“I’m going to bed,” she tells us, and then she’s gone.

Dad’s straight back on his phone. He pokes at it for a while until there’s no more footsteps above us.

“I’ll go check on the mutt,” he says. Then he, too, leaves.

I can hear his voice quietly in the kitchen, then the back door opens. A few minutes later it closes and quiet footsteps make their way upstairs. They’ll be in different rooms tonight, or she’ll kick up a fuss about him not finishing watching.

I sit and scroll until the credits roll, then turn off the TV. Grandpa’s asleep. His glass is empty on the side table next to him, and his glasses are half-way falling off his face.

I should wake him up, probably. Get him to go to bed.

I fold up the blanket and hang it over the sofa and turn off the lights before heading off to my room. Check my emails before I go to sleep. Delete the promotions and the subscriptions and the article, then turn off my phone and do my best to keep warm.

Maybe I’m still hungry, maybe I feel bad about leaving Grandpa down there, or maybe I just can’t sleep, but at four in the morning I wake up and go downstairs. I check in the sitting room, but he’s not in there, though his glass is. I pick it up and wander into the kitchen in search of a bowl of cereal. As soon as I turn the light on, I see her.

Damned Spot lies on the floor of the kitchen, wheezing harsh breaths in and out. A part of me knows that I should call my parents, that I should call the vet, but in the moment I just go to her and I sink to my knees and bury my hands in her fur.

“Good girl,” I tell her, as scared brown eyes meet mine. “Good dog. It’s alright.”

I stay there, stay slowly stroking her, as she goes still, spasms, goes still again.

“I want to bury her on the hill,” Mum insists, and so up we go while Dad carries Damned Spot, until we hit the cloud, just a bit lower than it was yesterday. Grandpa follows and his eyes watch everything.

“You know, we never buried our dogs,” he tells us, and I want to hit him or scream but I don’t do anything because we certainly never talk about the ways he’s awful in front of him or Mum.

Sam from the village is waiting up top with a digger by a freshly dug hole, only visible when we get close; he looms through cloud thick enough to make everything up here feel close and damp.

“Alright?” he says, sounding uncomfortable.

Dad thanks him, and Sam from the village nods before slowly driving back to the works over the road.

“I can’t bear it,” Mum informs us all, and staggers off by herself into the cloud.

That leaves Dad and me to lower her into the hole and push all the dirt on top, lay flat the grass turf, and shove in a stick to mark it.

“We should’ve brought a stone.”

“Should’ve had her cremated, really,” says Dad. “Much more efficient use of space. You know, they mix up all the ashes, scoop a bunch out and stick ‘em in a jar. ‘S not much point crying over a bunch of bits of other people’s pets.”

Grandpa’s standing off there in the mist, looking around as though thinking of all the places he’d rather be. “We never bothered with any of this, you know. Just told the vet to take it with them when he was done.”

Dad nudges me. “Maybe we should tell the doctor to do the same with him, hey?”

I don’t cry. I just stand there, as Grandpa goes wandering off. I’m glad for it, really. Glad he’s not saying anything else. I don’t think I could bear it.

There’s a moment where Dad and I stand around in the cloud, him silent and awkward and still waiting for me to cry or laugh, before he sighs and jerks his head. I step away and follow him, as we begin making our way after Mum.

She’s gone to the very top of the hill, where there’s a small trig point, just a bit of rock left to mark out the highest point, and is staring out into the endless, endlessly close fog.

“You know,” she says, and she sounds terribly far away. “I think I can see Wales.”

Dad takes her arm, guides her to lean on him, and the two begin to oh-so-slowly walk down the hill.

Grandpa touches my shoulder, and he won’t say it, but it is an apology. I keep my peace, and we follow them down.

They’re already in by the time we get there, boots on the rack, but nowhere to be seen.

“I’ll have a shower, I think,” Grandpa tells me and I’m ready for him to go upstairs but instead he follows me into the kitchen.

I watch him grab the washing-up liquid.

“Shower gel,” he says. Laughs, winks, and then he’s off with it in hand.

I stand there for a second. “What?”

But there’s only me in here now.

I never got that midnight snack, so I wander over to the fridge. Open it. The smell, unleashed, fills the room and I should shut the door and open the windows and put away Spot’s water bowl because she’ll not be needing it anymore and

I take the pack of chicken drumsticks out the fridge, slimy and discoloured and half-covered by a flapping lip of clear plastic that does nothing to stop the assault of their reek. And I put it on the counter and I leave it there to fill the whole room with its rot.

Here are the things that I’m going to do. I’m going to kick on the flip-flops by the door and I’m going to flip and flop my way outside and I will flip and flop my way all the way back up that hill. And I will lose a shoe three or four times; that’s inevitable. When I get there, I won’t be able to see Wales, but I will tell myself that up above me, amidst all the clouds, there’s a patch that’s a lighter shade of grey.

(By the time I come down, the chicken’s in the bin, uncovered, and the door to the kitchen’s shut. I can hear some nasally American accent coming from the sitting room, occasionally stuttering because the WiFi’s not so good in there. But that’s fine. I grab the bin bag and shove it — still open — into the hall.)

“You shouldn’t watch that stuff,” I tell him every time. Try to show as little reaction as possible.

“Always so serious,” he says. Then he turns it off. He’s got what he wanted, now he’ll get back to the crossword.

In the background, Grandpa sits in the corner. Can never tell if his hearing aid’s in or not, but that’s how he likes it. After all, another thing we never mention: he and Dad can’t stand each other. Grandpa used to play footie — now he’s an eighty-four-year-old conspiracy nut who wants to open all our eyes to the truth. Meanwhile Dad’s one YouTube Short from a full-on three-quarter-life crisis and doesn’t much like the vision he’s getting of his future. Deals with it by making it obvious he thinks Grandpa’s an old bigot (we also don’t talk about the pot meet kettle of it all).

“Frankie,” says Grandpa, “do you have a minute?”

Of course. “Of course.”

“Did you get my email?” he asks. Taps his tablet. “I sent you an article.”

The answer is yes, but I gave up at the headline: ‘Who Controls the Weather? How Governments Are Playing God With the Atmosphere.’

“Is it a pressing matter?” whispers Dad.

I give him a sideways glance. “I wouldn’t say that wisdom descended from above.”

Grandpa shakes his head. “You’ll have to repeat that, Frankie.”

“Oh, sorry.” I say. “It wasn’t anything interesting.”

He sits there for a moment. “Well, you ought to read the article.”

I glance behind me. Dad’s smirking, obviously. Best foot forward: I nod. Not enough. “I will?” That does it.

“That-a girl,” he tells me, and lets me go.

I can hear Mum making her way up the stairs, breathing heavily. The walk didn’t do her as much good as I’d hoped, but we try not to mention the fact that they never do. It’ll be a few days minimum before we can get her out again, now that it’s never sunny. Seasonal affective disorder gone mad.

Another truth unspoken: the electric bill’s gone haywire in the last few months. Mum’s always got the lights and the heating on upstairs, and we’ve got them on in the kitchen. Can’t complain about it, because it depresses her. Don’t want to sit in the dark.

Damned Spot looks up from her bed, struggles upright and limps to me, looking for a cuddle. I give her one. Used to be, even a week ago, she’d have followed Mum up to bed and lain at her feet for her nap. Didn’t even try to come on our walk today. I get my fingers right where she likes them, behind her ears, set her tail to its long, easy wags.

“Good girl,” I tell her firmly. By the door, her food bowl is picked at and she’s unreceptive to my attempts to get her to eat.

“Probably needs the loo,” my dad says.

I head for the door. “Out, Damned Spot?” I say, because that’s what we always say, and maybe her ears perk up. Or I’m just seeing what I want to. Either way, we stumble our five-legged way outside, where we stand on the grass under the low, thick grey of the sky for one minute, two, five.

Damned Spot stares around, brown-eyed and unquestioning, and doesn’t do her business or anything else. Eventually, tips of my fingers beginning to get cold, we stumble our five-legged way back in.

“Ought to be shot,” says Grandpa. “Kindest thing for it.”

Dad whistles her over and she goes to him, slow and struggling. “She’s got a bit of life in her yet,” he says, leans over to give her a proper stroke and nearly unbalances her. “Don’t you, girl?”

I go over to the fridge, open it, then shut it again before the smell of the chicken can escape.

“Snack supper?” I say and Dad laughs.

Mum’s been on the Austen miniseries again, decides we’re watching the new Persuasion ‘as a family’. Grandpa sits in the armchair with his whiskey and sips silently, eyes fixed on the far wall. Heating hasn’t been on in the sitting room for weeks and the damp’s got into the sofa so I’m buried under a blanket.

“Put it away,” Mum hisses. It’s more alive than I’ve heard her in a minute. Scares me out of my skin, and I do my best to look like I’m paying attention.

But I’m not the one in trouble. Dad sighs and puts his phone on the arm of the sofa next to him. Grandpa, in his chair, hums and sips.

It’s not a very good film.

Ten or so minutes pass before Mum stands up.

“I’m going to bed,” she tells us, and then she’s gone.

Dad’s straight back on his phone. He pokes at it for a while until there’s no more footsteps above us.

“I’ll go check on the mutt,” he says. Then he, too, leaves.

I can hear his voice quietly in the kitchen, then the back door opens. A few minutes later it closes and quiet footsteps make their way upstairs. They’ll be in different rooms tonight, or she’ll kick up a fuss about him not finishing watching.

I sit and scroll until the credits roll, then turn off the TV. Grandpa’s asleep. His glass is empty on the side table next to him, and his glasses are half-way falling off his face.

I should wake him up, probably. Get him to go to bed.

I fold up the blanket and hang it over the sofa and turn off the lights before heading off to my room. Check my emails before I go to sleep. Delete the promotions and the subscriptions and the article, then turn off my phone and do my best to keep warm.

Maybe I’m still hungry, maybe I feel bad about leaving Grandpa down there, or maybe I just can’t sleep, but at four in the morning I wake up and go downstairs. I check in the sitting room, but he’s not in there, though his glass is. I pick it up and wander into the kitchen in search of a bowl of cereal. As soon as I turn the light on, I see her.

Damned Spot lies on the floor of the kitchen, wheezing harsh breaths in and out. A part of me knows that I should call my parents, that I should call the vet, but in the moment I just go to her and I sink to my knees and bury my hands in her fur.

“Good girl,” I tell her, as scared brown eyes meet mine. “Good dog. It’s alright.”

I stay there, stay slowly stroking her, as she goes still, spasms, goes still again.

“I want to bury her on the hill,” Mum insists, and so up we go while Dad carries Damned Spot, until we hit the cloud, just a bit lower than it was yesterday. Grandpa follows and his eyes watch everything.

“You know, we never buried our dogs,” he tells us, and I want to hit him or scream but I don’t do anything because we certainly never talk about the ways he’s awful in front of him or Mum.

Sam from the village is waiting up top with a digger by a freshly dug hole, only visible when we get close; he looms through cloud thick enough to make everything up here feel close and damp.

“Alright?” he says, sounding uncomfortable.

Dad thanks him, and Sam from the village nods before slowly driving back to the works over the road.

“I can’t bear it,” Mum informs us all, and staggers off by herself into the cloud.

“Should’ve had her cremated, really,” says Dad. “Much more efficient use of space. You know, they mix up all the ashes, scoop a bunch out and stick ‘em in a jar. ‘S not much point crying over a bunch of bits of other people’s pets.”

Grandpa’s standing off there in the mist, looking around as though thinking of all the places he’d rather be. “We never bothered with any of this, you know. Just told the vet to take it with them when he was done.”

Dad nudges me. “Maybe we should tell the doctor to do the same with him, hey?”

I don’t cry. I just stand there, as Grandpa goes wandering off. I’m glad for it, really. Glad he’s not saying anything else. I don’t think I could bear it.

There’s a moment where Dad and I stand around in the cloud, him silent and awkward and still waiting for me to cry or laugh, before he sighs and jerks his head. I step away and follow him, as we begin making our way after Mum.

She’s gone to the very top of the hill, where there’s a small trig point, just a bit of rock left to mark out the highest point, and is staring out into the endless, endlessly close fog.

“You know,” she says, and she sounds terribly far away. “I think I can see Wales.”

Dad takes her arm, guides her to lean on him, and the two begin to oh-so-slowly walk down the hill.

Grandpa touches my shoulder, and he won’t say it, but it is an apology. I keep my peace, and we follow them down.

They’re already in by the time we get there, boots on the rack, but nowhere to be seen.

“I’ll have a shower, I think,” Grandpa tells me and I’m ready for him to go upstairs but instead he follows me into the kitchen.

I stand there for a second. “What?”

But there’s only me in here now.

I never got that midnight snack, so I wander over to the fridge. Open it. The smell, unleashed, fills the room and I should shut the door and open the windows and put away Spot’s water bowl because she’ll not be needing it anymore and

I take the pack of chicken drumsticks out the fridge, slimy and discoloured and half-covered by a flapping lip of clear plastic that does nothing to stop the assault of their reek. And I put it on the counter and I leave it there to fill the whole room with its rot.

They haven’t stopped shouting for three days, that rushing, rising mass of people pressing in at the walls of the stacks. They’re not there for the prisoners being shipped out today – petty criminals all, the real dregs of old Jovia. Not the sort of bastards worth causing trouble over. Now, Morrow doesn’t like to think of himself as a shining example of what Keth can be, but there’s something real nice and humbling about finding himself here among this company.

Out by the final gate, he can finally make out what the crowd has been saying.

“Udak adeekethe!”

The man leading the call has a good voice for it, even with the metallic edge of cheap amplification. Loud enough that even in the innermost stack, the outline of his words can still be felt in the shaking of the walls.

The response is unboosted, slurred at the edges by a crowd where only some of them know what the sounds they’re making even mean. “Adeeke de sodai ke!”

Nathan, cuffed to Morrow at the back of the column, takes a moment to lean in while the guards are distracted fitting masks on the men in front.

“What’s it mean?” he asks.

Morrow forgets, sometimes, that Nathan’s not Keth. Sure, he doesn’t look like it. He’s a head taller than anyone else in the lineup, pink cheeked and frail boned. But he moves like one. Weight low, shoulders hard. But no Keth would ever admit that they don’t know Kesh. Even if they don’t.

Morrow tilts his head to listen more closely to the chant.

“‘They’re taking our people’,” he says. The response is harder to parse. “What will –” no, not that. “‘Why won’t we fight now?’ Something like that.”

“You think they’ll still ship –”

He’s cut off as the guards get to them and strap ill fitting masks to their faces. There are too many eyes on them to talk. Nathan’s a line of tension next to him as they follow the men in front of them onto a transport bus. The guards sit them down next to each other at the back of the bus, attaching the chain connecting their wrists to bolts on the floor between their legs.

“Everyone on?” calls one of the guards.

Another flashes him a thumbs up, and the back door is swung closed and sealed.

There’s a moment of silence in the dark, the shuffling of bodies trying to fit themselves to their seats. Then the engine hums to life beneath and the strip lights come on and they all go still.

Morrow can tell exactly when they pass through the seal out onto Jovia proper. The bus judders, stops and starts, the voices rise up – not chanting anymore, just screaming wordlessly, slamming their hands against the metal.

They grind forward another foot, pressing through the unseen crowd. There’s the rough shouting of the guards, cries of pain from outside.

“Udak adeekethe!”

So clear and loud that it could only have come from inside the bus. Impossible to tell which of the masked, formless figures in the rows in front said it. It takes him a half second to remember the response.

“Adeeke de sodai ke!”

He’s not the only one who says it. Two other voices, all out of time with each other. But the first man calls out again, and they reply in sync, and this time they’re not the only ones. Morrow’s the closest to the guard at the back who drives his fist into his stomach. He gasps, winded, but Nathan takes up the response for him, the Kesh awkward in his mouth. Slams his boot against the floor in time, yanking Morrow’s ankle with him.

“Silence!” says the guard.

Morrow’s got his breath back, though, so when the call comes again, he joins in. They’re all stomping, all hitting the walls, and when they go again, he can hear some of the crowd outside shouting back.

The guard with them hits Morrow again, storming down the aisle towards the front with his baton, laying into the men on either side. But the crowd’s got their balance now. Doesn’t matter if one man or another can’t shout for a blow to the head, the sound is inescapable.

“Get us moving!” yells the guard, kicking the front of the compartment. For a second, there’s no response, and then they’re moving forward, crunching over something with a squeal of the suspension. They don’t stop. Someone screams outside, then others join in. No chanting out there, just panic. The guard grabs someone at the front, smacks his baton into the side of his head over and over until he goes limp, even as the man next to him kicks at his body armour. That gets him a punch to the throat.

“I said, shut the fuck up!” He keeps screaming it, even as they keep going with the chant. The partition opens and two men climb in from the front, and then there are three of them, sending blow after blow into the prisoners. Batons meeting throats, stomachs, heads. Morrow kicks at the groin of the man who makes his way back to him, tries to get as much of himself between them and Nathan as possible. But the guard thumbs the switch on the hilt, sends current seizing through him, leaving him twitching and stupid. There’s nothing he can do to guard either of them from the strikes that land along their sides and backs. No chance of chanting now, all his mouth is good for is silent, spasming gasps, as they thud the baton into him again and again and again.

Everyone’s quiet as they finally stand back from the beaten men. Morrow can’t move. Just hangs limp, mouth open as he gasps for air. The fucker who hit them, his mask’s slipped a bit. He’s got a sheen to his brown skin. Not sweat. Then he gets it back in place and straightens up. Same height as the other two. Same height as Morrow.

He tries to fling himself at them, but nothing in him listens. All he achieves is tipping himself off balance, flopping forward and out of his seat. Nathan does his best to pull him back up.

“Don’t,” he says.

The guard comes to stand over them. “Sit.”

He’s faceless through the smoked glass, breath wheezing through the air pipe.

“He’ll behave,” says Nathan. He’s got Morrow by the wrist where they’re joined, squeezing it tightly.

And it doesn’t even matter. Because the other guard smacks him in the head hard enough that he loses a few seconds. When the world comes back, two of them are pinning him to the seat while the other locks cuffs around his ankles, loops them into the hook. They smash another hit into his ribs before they walk away.

Morrow leans his head against the back of the chair, drooling a bit under the mask. No one’s talking anymore, no one’s moving. One of the guards goes back through the partition to the front, slides it shut behind him. The others take up posts at the front and the back. Hands on their batons.

Eventually they turn off from platform flatness onto a ramp.

The lordling’s lips twist. “It’s not.”

“I swore I’d find you,” he says. Holds out his arm. “No one in the capital has any answers; my father said  ”

I say nothing.

The nomads’ curd cheeses, their whey brew that burns the throat and leaves the little lord asleep well before the green flash. It’s a shame – his only chance to see it. They come to me one more time before they leave.
“No,” I tell them, before they can start.
“My father –” begins the lordling.
“Has nothing to offer me,” I tell him. “I have given him enough.” I shake my head, then look at his knife. “You could still go north.”
“You could still go south,” he says, and smiles. It’s freer now than the half-thing that he arrived with.
“No.” She says it with me.

“Soon.”

“Something in between, I think.” I smile at her. “Time enough for a few more dreams.”
“Hm. I’ll put the kettle on.”
I follow her inside.

“I was Aisker’s man when he hosted you at Dawnwatch.”
“Hm.” I wonder what he thinks now, if he still sees the half-sane creature I was then before she plucked me away to this place where I am more woman than dream. “And why are you here?”
“To protect his son.”
I say nothing.
“He wants you back.”
There’s the cutting edge, then. “Are you going to drag me back across the desert?” I ask. He could try, I suppose, though it surely won’t end happily.
“I’m meant to,” he says. “She’s the one who stole you?”
“If I am my own, then I give myself to her,” I say.
He leans on the balcony next to me. “If you’re right, I’m not sure anyone will care if I bring you back or not.”
“On this, I am.”
Now he’s silent, but I have the advantage – I know he’s about to speak.
“I’m glad you’ve found this,” he says.
His decision sets, and the dream sets with it. I dig a nail into a small crack in the wood. “If you were wise, you’d head north.” Pointless, I know.
“Does he make it home?”
“If you’re with him.”
“Then I’ll go with him.”
If I did want to go with them, to go back, would she let me? Would she follow? I won’t ask.
They do stay till Sunswap in the end. Even follow us up to Landsmeet. I watch them, as Father Sun reddens one horizon and Mother Sun pinks the other. It’s their first time meeting people who aren’t from Rest and aren’t sailors, and it’s been a long time since Dawnwatch was a port.
It seems to delight them. Music that still sounds otherworldly to me, even after half a lifetime of hearing it. The nomads’ curd cheeses, their whey brew that burns the throat and leaves the little lord asleep well before the green flash. It’s a shame – his only chance to see it. When it comes, it makes his companion jump, which makes me laugh into her neck. Even she smiles a bit. One sun sinks beneath the horizon, the other starts its climb.
They come to me one more time before they leave.
“No,” I tell them, before they can start.
“My father –” begins the lordling.
“Has nothing to offer me,” I tell him. “I have given him enough.” I shake my head, then look at his knife. “You could still go north.”
“You could still go south,” he says, and smiles. It’s freer now than the half-thing that he arrived with.
“No.” She says it with me.
The little lord looks like he wants to say something, but instead turns away. His oath sears itself into his flesh. Unfulfilled, it brands him with his choice.
They leave. The lordling to home, his knife to whatever happens to keep him from that home.
She leans against me, and I press a kiss to the side of her head.
“We’ll be done with the dream,” I tell her. “And we’ll go north to the end of the world where the suns go in circles around the horizon and people will think we’re mad when we tell them of the desert.”

“Soon.”

“Hm. I’ll put the kettle on.”
